title: BOCC Public Meeting Agenda - 10/15/26
text: David William Creade Jason T. LeeJ. M. Beeman, R. V. Caporale, Bennett, Atkinson, Brodie, Esq, Jr., CPA, President Commissioner Attorney Commissioner Administrator David J. Caporale, President William R. Atkinson, Commissioner Creade V. Brodie, Jr., Commissioner Jason M. Bennett, CPA, Administrator Board of County Commissioners David William Creade Jason T. LeeJ. M. Beeman, R. V. Caporale, Bennett, Atkinson, Brodie, Esq, Jr., CPA, President Commissioner Attorney Commissioner Administrator T. Lee Beeman, Esq, Attorney Public Business Meeting Agenda Thursday, October 15, 2026 - 5:00 PM Allegany County Office Building, 701 Kelly Road, Allegany Room 100 Cumberland, Maryland 21502 WE ASK THOSE CITIZENS WISHING TO ADDRESS THE BOARD TO REGISTER ON THE SIGN-UP SHEET AND CONDENSE THEIR COMMENTS TO FIVE MINUTES OR LESS. THIS WILL ALLOW AN OPPORTUNITY FOR EVERYONE WISHING TO COME FORWARD TO HAVE A CHANCE TO SPEAK. WE WILL CONDUCT OUR MEETING IN AN ORDERLY FASHION AND ASK THAT EVERYONE WISHING TO SPEAK FIRST BE RECOGNIZED BY THE PRESIDENT, COME TO THE MICROPHONE, AND GIVE HIS OR HER NAME AND ADDRESS PRIOR TO THEIR COMMENTS. 1. Pledge of Allegiance 2. Call to Order & Roll Call 3. Approval of Agenda 4. Statement of Closed Meeting A. The Board of County Commissioners did not meet in Closed Session on September 17, 2026. 5. Approval of Previous Meetings Minutes A. Approve the Public Business Meeting Minutes from September 17, 2026 6. Presentations A. Recognition Awards from the Sheriff - Sheriff Craig Robertson 7. Public Hearing 8. Action Agenda & Public Comment A. Award and Authorize County Staff to Sign the Contract for Engineering Design Services to The EADS Group to Perform a Valuation of the Utilities Owned by Maryland Water Services, Inc. - Adam Patterson, P.E., Director, Department of Public Works This will be in the amount of $35,000 from the general fund. B. Approve and Execute the Land and Water Conservation Fund Assistance Project Agreement Addendum P26AP01405 for the Notice of Award for the Willowbrook Outdoor Wellness Center Project – Phase II - Adam Patterson, P.E., Director, Department of Public Works The funding award is in the amount of $1,800,000. C. Approve the Distribution of Recycled Asphalt Millings for Road Improvement Projects on Non-County Maintained Public Roads - Adam Patterson, P.E., Director, Department of Public Works David William Creade Jason T. LeeJ. M. Beeman, R. V. Caporale, Bennett, Atkinson, Brodie, Esq, Jr., CPA, President Commissioner Attorney Attorne Commissioner Administrator Nine (9) requests met the eligibility requirements for the program, which equals a total of 1,026 tons of asphalt millings. D. Approve and Authorize Signatures on the PFund Superior Sales Contracts for EMS Division - Roger Bennett, Director, Department of Emergency Services This is a proposed three-year sales contract that will provide the County with a planned approach for replacing aging ambulances and maintaining a more reliable and sustainable EMS ambulance fleet. E. Approve and Authorize the County Administrator to Sign a Memorandum of Understanding with LaVale Rescue Squad for EMS Staffing and Billing - Roger Bennett, Director, Department of Emergency Services This obligates both the County EMS and LaVale Rescue Squad to provide medic assistance for a stipulated amount. F. Approve and Authorize the Surplus and Donation of an Ambulance to Mountain Maryland Search and Rescue - Roger Bennett, Director, Department of Emergency Services This ambulance belonged to the former Georges Creek Ambulance Service and our EMS Division has taken it out of service. G. Approve Labor-Management Agreement Between Local No. 1715 International Association of Firefighters and the Board of County Commissioners. - Roger Bennett, Director, Department of Emergency Services This Agreement governs the labor-management relationship between the Allegany County Department of Emergency Services and its employees, including wages, benefits, discipline, grievance procedure, promotion, and other rights and obligations. The Agreement will expire on June 30, 2029. H. Adopt Resolution 26-25 Replacement Job Descriptions for Bargaining Unit Positions of Local No. 1715 International Association of Firefighters and Allegany County Commissioners, Emergency Medical Services Division - Kristi Liller, Director, Department of Human Resources This is to approve replacement job descriptions for Emergency Medical Service union positions, as discussed during recent union negotiations. I. Authorize a Community Enhancement Program Grant to Town of Luke for Partial Payment for New Roof at Former Luke Post Office Building - David Nedved, Community Development Representative, Department of Economic and Community Development The quote to replace the roof with snow control and gutters is $23,742.50. The Town was approved for $12,500 from the Rocky Gap funds. Community Enhancement Program Funds would then make up the difference based on this quote, which is estimated at $11,242.50. J. Execute a Memorandum of Understanding with Archway Station for Eligible Project Costs for the Maryland Recovery Housing Project at 125 Fayette Street - David Nedved, Community Development Representative, Department of Economic and Community Development Allegany County would pay the Harbel Inc. bills only until the awarded CDBG funding is fully expended. K. Approve and Execute a Grant Agreement Between the Board of County Commissioners of Allegany County, Maryland and the Maryland Department of Commerce in the Amount of One Million Dollars ($1,000,000.00) for Rail Spur and Rail Infrastructure at Kingspan Roofing - Jeffrey S. Barclay, Director, Department of Economic & Community Development This Grant Agreement governs the terms of a Grant between Commerce and Allegany County related to the completion of rail spur and rail infrastructure improvements to occur on and near the property of Kingspan Roofing in the North Branch Industrial Park. L. Authorize Staff to Advertise and Solicit bids for Kingspan's Phase II Rail Project and Authorize up to $250,000 in RBF funds for Phase I and Phase II of the Project - Jeffrey S. Barclay, Director, Department of Economic and Community Development Phase I is the site work and Phase II is the laying of the rail siding to CSX specifications. This rail work convinced the company to locate here and leverages a $13 million building purchase and up to $30 David William Creade Jason T. LeeJ. M. Beeman, R. V. Caporale, Bennett, Atkinson, Brodie, Esq, Jr., CPA, President Commissioner Attorney Attorne Commissioner Administrator million in building improvements and equipment purchases by the company. The company has hired 16 employees to date and expects 95 total jobs in 3 years. 9. Consent Agenda & Public Comment A. Accept and Authorize the Sheriff to Sign Documentation for the FY27 SRO Adequate Coverage Grant in the amount of $84,384 This funding will help supplement the salaries of 4 full-time SRO positions, as well as overtime pay for police officers to provide adequate coverage for 12 schools. B. Approve the Sale of Surplus and Abandoned Vehicles from the Sheriff's Office These vehicles will be sold at auction by GovDeals. C. Authorize Payment of Allegany County Narcotics Taskforce Invoice to LeadsOnline in the amount of $7,100 This annual software licensing fee is to be paid from the segregated forfeiture funds of the Allegany County Narcotics Taskforce. D. Award Bartlett Run Road Paving as an Extension of the State Aid Paving Contract ACRD-26-01 with Belt Paving, Inc. This will utilize the unit prices from the public bid process in the amount of $69,199.10. 10. General Public Comment 11. Reports A. County Administrator B. County Attorney 12. Commissioner Comments 13. Reminders/Upcoming Meetings A. Anticipated BOCC Public Work Session - Thursday, November 12, 2026 (Details and Time TBA) B. BOCC Public Business Meeting - Thursday, November 12, 2026, 5:00pm 14. Adjournment

title: Agenda 10-5-26
text: COUNTY COUNCIL OF ANNE ARUNDEL COUNTY, MARYLAND AGENDA Legislative Session 2026, Legislative Day No. 18 Monday, October 5, 2026 – 6:00 P.M. County Council Chambers 44 Calvert Street Annapolis, Maryland A. Call to Order B. Invocation (Rodvien) C. Pledge of Allegiance D. Citation Presentation E. Ethics Statement F. Invitation to Audience G. Announcement of Items Not Appearing on Agenda H. Preliminary Motion I. Approval of Minutes September 21, 2026 – Legislative Day No. 17 J. Introduction of Bills K. Introduction of Resolutions RESOLUTION NO. 34-26 – RESOLUTION supporting the Anne Arundel County Board of Education’s Fiscal Year 2028 Public School Construction Capital Improvement Program request for submission to the Interagency Commission on School Construction Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) RESOLUTION NO. 35-26 – RESOLUTION approving Anne Arundel County’s 2026 Financial Assurance Plan for compliance with the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination Phase I Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System Permit Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) RESOLUTION NO. 36-26 – RESOLUTION approving the revision of certain terms and conditions of the private disposition of certain County-owned property in Glen Burnie, Maryland, known as 7409 Baltimore-Annapolis Boulevard Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) Agenda October 5, 2026 Page 2 L. Public Hearings and Call of Bills and Resolutions for Final Reading and/or Vote BILL NO. 59-26 (As Amended) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Conflicts of Interest – County Council – FOR the purpose of amending the definition of “legislative action”; defining “participation”; expanding the types of presumed conflicts of interest that would prohibit a Councilmember from participating in legislative action to include Councilmembers and their immediate family members; and generally relating to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 63-26 (As Amended) (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – Data Storage Center – FOR the purpose of modifying the definition of “data storage center”; grandfathering certain data storage centers; removing certain parking requirements for data storage centers; removing certain data storage centers as an allowable use in certain commercial, industrial, mixed use, and Odenton Town Center districts; removing the conditional use requirements for certain data storage centers; making certain technical and stylistic changes; and generally related to zoning. FOR the purpose of repealing the personal property tax assessment reduction for qualified data storage centers; enacting a temporary moratorium on actions related to the development of data storage centers in Anne Arundel County and enacting legislation relating to the regulation of data storage centers in Anne Arundel County; requiring the formation of a work group to consider matters relating to the regulation of data storage centers in the County and to prepare a report and recommendations to the County Executive and the County Council regarding regulation of data storage centers in the County; and generally relating to data storage centers. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 66-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Enforcement – County Council – FOR the purpose of authorizing the Ethics Commission to impose a civil penalty for a violation of the public ethics law; authorizing the Ethics Commission to dispose of a complaint by consent order; establishing procedures for the assessment, collection, waiver, and reduction of a civil penalty imposed by the Ethics Commission; allowing for judicial review of a final order of the Ethics Commission for certain unpaid civil penalties; and generally relating to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 67-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Zoning – BWI Mixed Use Overlay Area – FOR the purpose of amending the BWI Mixed Use Overlay Area Map; and generally relating to zoning. Introduced by Mr. Smith BILL NO. 70-26 (Amendment Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Boards, Commissions, and Similar Bodies – Subdivision and Development – Concept Plan – FOR the purpose of requiring the Odenton Town Center Advisory Committee to review and make advisory opinions on certain concept plans; establishing an optional concept plan process in lieu of a sketch plan or preliminary plan in certain circumstances, establishing an application fee for and a review process of concepts plan applications; requiring concept plan applications be posted on the County’s webpage; allowing a developer to proceed directly to a final plan or site development plan application after following a certain concept Agenda October 5, 2026 Page 3 plan application process; and generally relating to boards, commissions, and similar bodies and subdivision and development. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) BILL NO. 61-26 (As Amended) (Amendment(s) Proposed) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Safety – Zoning – Article 18 Update – FOR the purpose of adding and modifying definitions of certain terms; removing the definitions of certain obsolete terms; revising certain general provisions; providing for the scope, administration, and interpretation of the Zoning Code; adding legacy provisions applicable to certain development applications and zoning certificates of use; establishing certain requirements for zoning certificate of use applications; establishing exemptions to bulk regulations for dwellings in existence as of a certain date; modifying certain parking space requirements; modifying certain temporary parking area criteria; adding purpose clauses for certain zoning districts; modifying, adding, and removing certain uses allowed in certain zoning districts under certain circumstances; clarifying certain bulk regulations in certain districts; removing the Open Space Conservation Overlay as obsolete; modifying certain requirements for certain conditional uses; modifying certain requirements for certain special exception uses; modifying certain provisions pertaining to certain special uses; modifying certain provisions pertaining to nonconforming uses; establishing standards for decisions on nonconforming use applications and prohibiting subsequent nonconforming use applications; modifying certain provisions pertaining to applications and hearings before the Administrative Hearing Officer; clarifying the requirements for keeping a variance or special exception from expiring; modifying certain provisions pertaining to certain enforcement and penalties; clarifying certain existing provisions; making certain technical and stylistic changes; correcting references to State Code provisions; correcting certain cross-references; and generally relating to public safety, and zoning. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) BILL NO. 65-26 (As Amended) – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Ethics – Campaign Contribution Disclosure and Comprehensive Zoning Integrity Act – FOR the purpose of adding a definition for “applicant”, “ benefit financially”, “covered person”, and “zoning text amendment”; requiring certain campaign contribution disclosures from applicants for certain land use determinations, zoning text amendment legislation, and land use legislative actions; prohibiting certain campaign contributions during certain zoning processes; providing for a delayed effective date; and generally related to public ethics. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 68-26 – AN EMERGENCY ORDINANCE concerning: Capital Budget and Program – Town Center to Reece Road and Culvert Invert Paving Capital Projects – Transfer of Appropriations – FOR the purpose of amending the Capital Budget for the current fiscal year by transferring an appropriation of funding from the Town Cntr to Reece Rd capital project to the Culvert Invert Paving capital project; amending the Capital Program and Capital Projects Bond Ordinance for the current fiscal year; making this Ordinance an emergency measure; and generally relating to appropriation of funds in projects in the Capital Budget for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) Agenda October 5, 2026 Page 4 BILL NO. 69-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Personnel – Positions in the Classified Service – Positions in the Exempt Service – Public Ethics – Financial Disclosure – Health Department – Police Department – FOR the purpose of adding a job classification to the exempt service; requiring a certain job classification in the exempt service to file a financial disclosure statement with the Ethics Commission; decreasing certain positions in the classified service and increasing certain positions in the classified and exempt service within the Health Department and the Police Department; and generally relating to personnel and public ethics. Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) BILL NO. 71-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Neighborhood Preservation and Environmental Protection Act – FOR the purpose of exempting required open area from the modification process; reverting certain density requirements to be net density; modifying a certain plat dedication to require offsite open area to be nearest to the subdivision; modifying certain open and active recreation area requirements; modifying the definition of attached dwelling; modifying active recreation area requirements; modifying certain allowed and prohibited uses in the Parole Town Center; removing definitions of and references to triplex, fourplex, multiplex and stacked townhouse dwelling units; modifying the definitions of duplex and multifamily dwelling; adding a definition of semi-detached dwelling; modifying certain parking requirements and bulk regulations regarding certain dwelling types; modifying certain bulk regulations in certain zoning districts; removing triplex, fourplex, multiplex and stacked townhouse dwelling units as allowable uses in all zoning districts, and the Commercial Revitalization Area Overlay; removing multifamily dwellings as a conditional use in certain residential districts; making duplex and semi-detached dwellings a special exception use or permitted use in certain residential and Odenton Town Center zoning districts; removing duplex dwellings as a permitted use in mixed use zoning districts; removing the conditional use requirements for a multifamily dwelling in certain residential districts; removing the conditional use requirements for triplex, fourplex, multiplex and stacked townhouse dwellings; establishing conditional use and special exception use requirements for duplex and semi-detached dwellings; modifying the special exception use requirements for an assisted living facility; modifying the density bonus permitted in certain circumstances; making certain technical and stylistic changes; and generally relating to public works, subdivision and development, and zoning. Introduced by Mr. Volke BILL NO. 72-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Construction and Property Maintenance Codes – International Swimming Pool and Spa Code – Barrier Requirements – FOR the purpose of removing the exemption to certain barriers for pools with powered safety covers; and generally relating to construction and property maintenance codes. Introduced by Ms. Fiedler BILL NO. 73-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Finance, Taxation, and Budget – Real Property Tax – Tax Credits – Surviving Spouses of Disabled Veterans or Individuals who Died in the Line of Active Military Duty Who Do Not Qualify for Certain Other Tax Credits – FOR the purpose of providing for a tax credit for surviving spouses of disabled veterans or individuals who died in the line of active military duty who do not qualify for Agenda October 5, 2026 Page 5 certain other tax credits in certain circumstances; and generally relating to finance, taxation, and budget. Introduced by Ms. Leadbetter BILL NO. 74-26 – AN ORDINANCE concerning: Public Safety – Miscellaneous Provisions – Repeal of Paper and Reusable Bags Fee Requirement – FOR the purpose of repealing the requirement to charge for paper bags and certain duties of retail establishments; repealing the violation of failure to charge, collect, or retain fees per paper and reusable carryout bags; and generally relating to public safety. Introduced by Mr. Volke, Ms. Leadbetter, and Ms. Fiedler RESOLUTION NO. 32-26 – RESOLUTION confirming the appointment of a County resident and a member of the classified service to serve on the Pension Oversight Commission for Anne Arundel County Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) RESOLUTION NO. 33-26 – RESOLUTION approving submission of names for the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board Introduced by Ms. Hummer, Chair (by request of the County Executive) M. Other Business N. Adjournment ACCESSIBILITY POLICY Anyone with a disability who requires a reasonable accommodation to fully participate in a Council meeting should contact the Administrative Officer at least 72 hours before the meeting to discuss your accessibility needs. The Administrative Officer may be reached by email at ccschu24@aacounty.org or by telephone at 410-222-1401. TTY users, please call Maryland Relay via 7-1-1. Council meetings are also broadcast on Arundel TV. To find a list of local cable channels or to access Arundel TV you may visit:www.aacounty.org/services-and-programs/governmenttelevision. Broadcast Information City Council meetings are broadcast live on Tuesday nights on Comcast Cable Channel 71 and Verizon Channel 25. The most recent meeting is rebroadcast on those stations at the following times: ▪ Monday through Friday at 9:00 a.m. (please note that the rebroadcasts on Wednesdays at 9:00 a.m. are from the previous week; the first rebroadcast of the Tuesday Council Meeting is on Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m.) ▪ Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. ▪ Thursdays and Fridays at 6:00 p.m. ▪ Saturdays at 10:00 a.m. Next Mayor and Council Meeting: October 20, 2026 Proclamation Breast Cancer Awareness Month 005 City of College Park National Breast Cancer Awareness Month October 2026 PROCLAMATION WHEREAS, October 2026 is recognized as National Breast Cancer Awareness Month, an annual campaign to raise awareness, encourage early detection, and support those affected by breast cancer; and WHEREAS, breast cancer remains one of the most common cancers affecting women, making education, routine screenings, and access to quality care essential to improving outcomes and saving lives; and WHEREAS, continued research, advances in treatment, and community support have improved survival rates, while increasing awareness helps empower individuals to take proactive steps toward breast health; and WHEREAS, the City of College Park encourages residents to participate in educational programs, screenings, fundraising events, and other initiatives that support breast cancer awareness, research, and those impacted by the disease; and NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED that the Mayor and City Council of the City of College Park hereby proclaim October 2026 as Breast Cancer Awareness Month and urge all residents to promote awareness, support those affected by breast cancer, and join efforts to advance prevention, early detection, and research. PROCLAIMED this 6th day of October , 2026. ___ Fazlul Kabir, Mayor City of College Park 006 Proclamation Grant for Safe Schools Day 007 PROCLAMATION City of College Park, Maryland GRANTS FOR SAFE SCHOOLS DAY WHEREAS, the Greenlights Grant Initiative recognizes Grants for Safe Schools Day as an opportunity to raise awareness of available funding to support school safety; and WHEREAS, federal grants can provide critical resources for school security improvements, mental health services, and other programs that support safe and supportive learning environments; and WHEREAS, the Greenlights Grant Initiative provides school districts with guidance, resources, and training to help them identify and pursue funding opportunities; and WHEREAS, investing in safe and supportive schools strengthens the well-being of students, staff, families, and the communities they serve; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED by the Mayor and Council of the City of College Park that the 6th day of October 2026 is recognized as Grants for Safe Schools Day supporting the Greenlights Grant Initiative and encourage awareness and support of efforts to help schools access funding for safety and security initiatives. PROCLAIMED this 6th day of __October , 2026. ___ Fazlul Kabir, Mayor City of College Park 008 Proclamation Indigenous Peoples Day 009 PROCLAMATION City of College Park, Maryland Indigenous Peoples’ Day WHEREAS, Indigenous Peoples' Day will be observed on Monday, October 12, 2026, honoring the histories, cultures, traditions, and contributions of Indigenous Peoples throughout the Americas; and WHEREAS, Indigenous Peoples have stewarded these lands since time immemorial, and their enduring resilience, knowledge, and cultural heritage continue to enrich our communities and nation; and WHEREAS, the lands that are now Maryland have long been home to Indigenous Peoples, including the Piscataway, Algonquin, Iroquois, and Sioux peoples, whose histories and legacies remain an important part of our shared heritage; and WHEREAS, Indigenous Peoples' Day provides an opportunity to recognize the lasting contributions of Indigenous communities while promoting education, understanding, and respect for their cultures, histories, and traditions; and NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED by the Mayor and City Council of the City of College Park that Monday, October 12, 2026, is hereby recognized as Indigenous Peoples' Day and all residents are encouraged to honor the rich histories, cultures, and contributions of Indigenous Peoples. City Engineer Meeting Date: October 6, 2026 Presented By: Steven Halpern City Engineer Consent Agenda: Yes Originating Department: Department of Public Works Action Requested: Consideration of approval of a task order under the on-call engineering services contract with Charles P. Johnson and Associates (CPJ). in the amount of $129,410.00 for the design of the Branchville Road - 51st Avenue Sidewalk Project Strategic Plan Objective: Objective 7: Expand and promote alternative transportation approaches to build a more interconnected and accessible City for all. Background/Justification: In 2018 the City developed a priority matrix to identify sidewalk projects that support the City’s Complete and Green Streets initiatives. Branchville Road - 51st Avenue - was identified as one of the top priority sidewalk connectivity routes. This sidewalk project will complete the pedestrian route from University Boulevard to the recently completed sidewalk along 52nd Avenue. This will complete the pedestrian sidewalk to the Greenbelt Metro Station from University Boulevard. Engineering staff solicited and received design proposals from our on-call engineering consultants Rummel Klepper & Kahl, LLP (RK&K), Charles P Johnson and Associates (CPJ), and Greenman-Pederson, Inc. (GPI). Cost proposals are as flows: Charles P Johnson and Associates (CPJ): Rummel Klepper & Kahl, LLP (RK&K): Greenman-Pederson, Inc. (GPI): $129,410.00 $138,783.83 $227,961.44 It is anticipated that the design and permitting will take about one year to complete. CPJ’s proposal is attached. Fiscal Impact: The Branchville Road - 51st Avenue Sidewalk was approved in the FY 2027 budget. It is funded in the Completed and Green Streets CIP. Equity & Inclusion Impact: The implementation of additional sidewalks helps make the City a more accessible and safer place to live. Council Options: 1. Approve the recommended task order with CPJ in the amount of $129,410.00 2. Request additional information from staff and bring this item back to a future work session. 3. Do not move forward with the design of the project. Staff Recommendation: 1. Option #1 - Approve the recommended task order with CPJ in the amount of $129,410.00 012 Recommended Motion: I move to approve and authorize the City Manager to execute a task order under the on-call engineering services contract with Charles P. Johnson and Associates (CPJ). in the amount of $129,410.00 for the design of the Branchville Road - 51st Avenue Sidewalk Project, subject to the review of the City Attorney. Johnson & Associates, Inc. (CPJ) is pleased to submit our fee proposal for the design of the proposed 5-foot-wide sidewalk along Branchville Road and 51st Avenue, from the intersection of University Boulevard and Rhode Island Avenue to David Hall. CPJ understands that the final sidewalk alignment will be selected with community input and that the project includes two community meetings and up to two Council presentations. Our scope includes project kickoff and data collection, topographic survey, evaluation of sidewalk alternatives, preliminary grading and utility impact analysis, right-of-way review, preparation of 60% and 90% design plans, maintenance of traffic plans, drainage design, engineer’s estimates, specifications, quality control reviews, and final bid-ready construction documents. Based on coordination with the City, this proposal assumes that stormwater management facilities, permitting, and construction administration services are not included. CPJ appreciates the opportunity to continue supporting the City of College Park and looks forward to working with the City and community stakeholders to advance this important pedestrian improvement project. He stated that the grant would assist with substantial redevelopment costs and requested that the Council continue considering the grant. Angela Gentile, resident, provided an update on efforts to reestablish the College Park Boys and Girls Club and thanked the Mayor and Councilmembers for their assistance. Ms. Bailey Hedgepeth also highlighted the City’s efforts to welcome conference attendees, including installation of "Welcome to Quantum" and “CP Loves Quantum” banners throughout the City. The most recent meeting is rebroadcast on those stations at the following times:  Monday through Friday at 9:00 a.m. (please note that the rebroadcasts on Wednesdays at 9:00 a.m. are from the previous week; the first rebroadcast of the Tuesday Council Meeting is on Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m.)  Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m.  Thursdays and Fridays at 6:00 p.m.  Saturdays at 10:00 a.m. Next Mayor and Council Meeting: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 @7:30 p.m. 3 A Education and Literacy Overview 004 CITY OF COLLEGE PARK, MARYLAND WORKSESSION AGENDA ITEM Prepared By: Kiaisha Barber Meeting Date:10/20/2026 Youth, Family and Senior Services Director Vincent Johns, Education Consultant Melinda Coles, Education Consultant Presented By: Kiaisha Barber Consent Agenda: No Originating Department: Youth, Family and Senior Services Action Requested: Feedback on Education and Literacy Priorities and Recommendations Strategic Plan Goal: OKR #9 Advocate for improving the quality of education and learning opportunities for our residents and community’s future. The Mayor and Council Budget for Public School Education Initiatives is $152,250 in Fiscal Year 2027. Following a presentation to Mayor and Council on these current education initiatives and programs on 8/6/2026, the following education initiatives have explored by staff and two education consultants. 1. Examine existing tutoring programs, specifically $30,000 budgeted annually for the online tutoring platform Imagine Learning, and make recommendations regarding continuation or other tutoring possibilities 2. Revise Public School Education Grant Eligibility 3. Revise the eligibility for Summer Camp Scholarship Program and Improve Data Collection and Program Evaluation 4. Strengthen Family Education and Resource Navigation 5. Establish an Adult ESL Program 6. Facilitate PGCPS School Volunteer Registration The list was used as a starting point to determine feasibility based on importance, community need, available staff time, cost, potential partnerships, and anticipated impact. Each initiative is listed along with staff and education consultant supported recommendations for next steps. 1. Examine existing tutoring programs, specifically $30,000 budgeted annually for the online tutoring platform Imagine Learning, and make recommendations regarding continuation or other tutoring possibilities. The City of College Park currently allocates $30,000 in the FY2027 budget to provide residents with access to Imagine Learning for academic support, GED preparation, and ACT/SAT preparation. However, as of September 22, 2026, an analysis of the platform’s 68 registered student profiles found that no participants had completed a module. Approximately 120 accounts had initially been created, including duplicate accounts. Low engagement may reflect the availability of alternative resources, including: o Existing school-based programs: Residents have access to tutoring through programs such as Hollywood Aspire, Paint Branch Lakeland STARs, the Buck Lodge Latino Student Fund Saturday Tutoring Program, Greenbelt CARES, and tutoring programs at Parkdale High School and the University of Maryland. o Free virtual tutoring through Brainfuse: The Prince George’s County Memorial Library System provides free one-on-one tutoring in English and Spanish, along with self-guided 005 learning resources. Prince George’s County Public Schools also recommends Brainfuse to families through its school websites. Given the availability of comparable free resources and the lack of recorded module completion on Imagine Learning, we recommend discontinuing the platform partnership and reallocating the existing $30,000 toward direct academic support, expanded tutoring capacity, and enrichment opportunities for College Park residents. Short-Term Recommendations o Discontinue Imagine Learning and Promote Brainfuse  Discontinue the City’s Imagine Learning partnership and promote Brainfuse as a free alternative for residents seeking virtual tutoring and academic support. The City should publicize this resource through its website, community events, and education outreach booth to increase awareness and access. o Establish School-Based Tutoring Grants: $7500  Allocate additional tutoring monies to Buck Lodge Middle School, Parkdale High School, and College Park Academy to support existing or expanded tutoring programs. Eligible expenses would include instructional materials, books, snacks, and other direct program costs.  Funding should be tied to the number of College Park residents served, ensuring that City resources benefit local residents even though the schools are county-run or independently operated.  Each participating school should report resident participation, overall attendance, and student academic growth using pre- and post-assessments. o Create an Official Partnership with the Latino Student Fund and Create STEM Saturdays: $10000  Invest $10,000 in the Latino Student Fund’s STEM Saturday partnership, which operates within College Park and provides tutoring and academic enrichment. The program currently serves approximately 90 students and has a waiting list of 45, demonstrating existing demand for additional services.  The program has reported approximately 25% improvement in student assessment outcomes from pre-assessment to post-assessment. Through its TE GUIO STEM Program and Listo College Access Program, the Latino Student Fund could expand its Saturday program to provide ACT/SAT preparation, hands-on STEM workshops, and college readiness programming to its College Park location. This directly supports the city’s educational goals.  The proposed investment would expand capacity from 90 to 130 students. Funding would support instructional materials, 20 computers, meals and snacks, and an additional program needs.  The organization should report enrollment, overall attendance, the number of College Park residents served, and student growth to document program reach and effectiveness. o Expand Elementary Academic Support: $12500  Expand access to high-dosage tutoring for elementary students who need additional academic support. Programs such as Amplify Tutoring have demonstrated promising results at Hollywood Elementary, where College Park residents represent the largest share of enrollment of any school.  Students participating in the Amplify Tutoring Program improved their assessment outcomes by approximately 24% on average and demonstrated growth at rates exceeding those of their peers.  The City could award the proposed funds through an open application process to qualified organizations with a demonstrated record of improving student learning outcomes. Funding should prioritize expanding access to students who need additional support. This investment could initially operate as a pilot program. Participating organization(s) should measure student growth using pre- and post2 006 assessments and, where feasible, compare outcomes with those of similar students who do not participate in the program. Findings should inform future funding decisions. Accountability and Evaluation All funded programs should report the number of College Park residents served, student attendance, and academic growth measured through pre- and post-assessments. Where feasible, programs should also evaluate outcomes against an appropriate comparison group. These reporting requirements will allow the City to assess program reach, evaluate student outcomes, and make evidence-based funding decisions in future years. Recommendation Discontinue the Imagine Learning partnership and reallocate the existing $30,000 toward schoolbased tutoring, the Latino Student Fund STEM Saturday partnership, and expanded elementary academic support. This approach prioritizes programs with existing demand and opportunities for direct student engagement while establishing measurable outcomes to guide future City investments in education. 2. Revise Public School Education Grant Eligibility Since 2008, the Mayor and Council have provided grant monies to public neighborhood boundary schools for City of College Park students. The purpose of the grants is to support the local neighborhood schools by enriching students’ educational experience and enhancing College Park neighborhoods. Grant amounts are available in two tiers. The tier one schools are identified as the four neighborhood boundary schools with the most College Park students and may receive up to $8,000. The tier two schools are additional City neighborhood boundary schools which have 14 or more College Park students and may receive up to $2,750. The tier is determined by the number of College Park students in their school as of October of the previous school year. Additionally, in FY 2018, Council voted to allow College Park Academy to be eligible for up to $2,250 for a grant to support educational needs of students and/or the school community of College Park’s neighborhood public schools. The four tier one schools, eligible for a grant up to $8,000, are Hollywood Elementary, Paint Branch Elementary, Buck Lodge Middle and Parkdale High. The current additional City neighborhood boundary schools that enroll 14 or more College Park students, eligible for up to $2,750, are Berwyn Heights Elementary, Cherokee Lane Elementary, University Park Elementary, Beltsville Academy, Greenbelt Middle, Hyattsville Middle School and High Point High School. In October of each year, Prince George’s County Public Schools provides school and enrollment information to the City. This information is used for budget purposes for the following fiscal year. The most recent information from PGCPS indicates the current College Park resident boundary schools and their enrollment of College Park students to be: • • Elementary Schools: o Beltsville Academy, K-8: 26 o Berwyn Heights: 36 o Cherokee Lane: 72 o Hollywood: 289 o Paint Branch: 252 o Riverdale: <10 o University Park: 23 Middle Schools: o Buck Lodge: 175 o Greenbelt: 69 3 007 • • o Hyattsville: 16 High Schools: o High Point: 48 o Northwestern: 10 o Parkdale: 257 *College Park Academy: 68 Schools have annually been given broad guidelines on how they may use grant funds. Recommendation Revising the categories and areas for which the grant can be used allows the City to clearly state how the grant funds support targeted areas of its boundary schools. The following categories are recommended exclusively for schools. The recommendation is for these categories to be implemented this fiscal year, with applications made available in early November. Academic Support: textbooks and instructional materials, tutoring, STEM or ESL support, test preparation School Clubs and Student Organizations: start-up or ongoing support for clubs, advisors’ supplies, competitions Athletics: equipment, uniforms, training spaces, team support Capital Improvement (Facilities): equipment or improvements to buildings, grounds, labs, libraries, or fitness spaces School Events and Student Engagement: events, assemblies, field trips, recognition programs, school culture Student Support: attendance, mentoring, counseling support, college and career readiness Family and Community Engagement: PTA support, parent nights, family resources, community events Fully revised draft grant applications are provided as an appendix to this report. 3. Revise the eligibility for Summer Camp Scholarship Program Annually the Council supports scholarships open to any student who is a resident of College Park. Specifically, youth (rising K-12) who reside in the City of College Park are eligible to apply. Scholarships are granted up to a maximum of $400 per student Recommendation The recommendation for the Youth Summer Camp Scholarship is to add a financial need requirement to the Youth Summer Camp Scholarship Application. As well, applications should be made available in January of each year. Financial need can be demonstrated through documentation such as: • Temporary Cash Assistance • Supplemental Security Income • Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) • Maryland Medicaid • Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB) • Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB) • Free or Reduced Lunch with the school system (CCBOE) 4 008 For applicants who do not have this documentation, a separate hardship form will allow them to describe their financial hardship and provide supporting evidence, so families without the listed documentation can still qualify. 300% of the Federal Poverty Level should be used as guidance, not an absolute cutoff, so the requirement remains flexible for individual family circumstances. This approach is modeled on eligibility and processing methods used by comparable jurisdictions. Some comparable programs across the region and nation include: • City of Hyattsville, MD The Hyattsville Children & Youth Camp Scholarship provides financial assistance to families of Hyattsville residents in grades K–5 who demonstrate financial need and need support participating in City youth programs. Eligible scholarships may cover Spring Break Camp, the Night Owls Program, and up to four weeks of Summer Camp, including extended-hour coverage. Applicants must provide proof of residency, the child’s birth certificate, a parent/guardian’s government-issued ID, and documentation demonstrating financial need through government assistance, household income, or financial hardship. Applications are submitted online through RecDesk, and new applicants must create an account. • Montgomery County, MD Rec Assist Summer Camp Scholarship The Montgomery County Rec Assist Fund provides $400 per eligible family member to qualifying Montgomery County residents who receive certain public assistance or attend an eligible Montgomery County Public School. Funds are available for up to 12 months or until depleted and can be used toward Recreation programs and activities costing $25 or more, including summer camps, sports, swimming, art, dance, and fitness programs. Participants must pay a minimum 20% copayment, and funds are distributed on a first-come, first-served basis. Applications are typically processed within 10 business days, and assistance may only be used by eligible family members. • Worcester County, MD Summer Activities for At-Risk Youth GOLD’s Summer Activities for At-Risk Youth Program provides scholarships to help youth in Worcester County participate in summer camps and other enrichment activities. To qualify, youth must reside in Worcester County and live in a low-income household, defined as household income at or below 200% of the Federal Poverty Level. Eligibility is based on household size and gross monthly income, with the income limit increasing for each additional household member. • Charles County, MD RecAssist The Charles County RecAssist Program provides an annual $200 recreation program credit to Charles County residents who demonstrate eligibility through participation in approved assistance programs, including SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, Temporary Cash Assistance, and free or reduced-price school meals. Participants must provide proof of residency and eligibility and pay a minimum 20% co-payment per program. Funding is available on a first-come, first-served basis until funds are depleted, and assistance is subject to program space and availability. • City of Doraville, GA Summer Camp Scholarship The City of Doraville Summer Camp Scholarship provides eligible families with a $500 camp voucher per child on a first-come, first-served basis. Families must apply in person at Forest Fleming Arena and provide a valid ID and acceptable income verification, such as Medicaid, PeachCare, EBT/SNAP, Free/Reduced Lunch documentation, or a signed 2021 tax return listing the child as a dependent. Income limits are $60,000 for a family of two, $65,000 for three, and $70,000 for four or more. Scholarships are non-transferable, non-refundable, and may only be used at the Doraville Summer Camp location. 5 009 4. Strengthen Family Education and Resource Navigation The education consultant assessed available family resources surrounding navigating the education opportunities for themselves and their children living in College Park with the goal of ensuring College Park families have access to: o Assistance navigating school options, enrollment requirements, application deadlines, scholarships, and other educational resources. o Increased outreach where there may be less awareness of available opportunities, including Spanish-speaking families. The consultant also explored whether this should be provided by City staff, the Education Support Considerations: Community need, staff time, language access, cost, and whether existing community resources could be leveraged. Findings: Prince George’s County Public Schools (PGCPS) provides a wide array of family education resources for families, including Spanish-speaking families. PGCPS currently has both school-based (Appendix A) and county-wide (Appendix B) options available to provide families with assistance navigating school options, enrollment requirements, application deadlines,

Strategic Plan Goal: Objective 6: Inspire and nurture a welcoming and inclusive community that encourages and embodies engagement, collaboration, and equity throughout our City. Background/Justification: In 2013, the Mayor and Council established the Jack Perry Award in recognition of Councilmember John Edward “Jack” Perry, who served on the City Council for a total of 26 years and was actively involved in the community from the time he moved to Berwyn in 1969 until his death in 2012. The resolution establishing the award provides for recognition of a College Park resident who has demonstrated extraordinary participation in neighborhood, civic, or municipal affairs in a manner that improves public spaces, fosters community cohesion, eradicates blight, informs public discussion, provides leadership, and/or furthers the best interests of the City as a whole. The nomination period is open annually and is publicized in the Municipal Scene, the College Park Here and Now newspaper, on the City’s website, and in the weekly bulletin. A subcommittee consisting of Karyn Keating, Dan Blasberg, Jen DiStefano, and Donna Long met virtually to review the nominations. Following its review, the subcommittee unanimously recommended Robert Thurston as the recipient of the 2026 Jack Perry Award. Four nominations for Mr. Thurston are attached. The resolution establishing the award provides that the subcommittee’s recommendation must be forwarded to the full Council for approval by majority vote. Fiscal Impact: N/A Council Options: 1. Approve the nomination of Robert Thurston. 2. Do not approve the nomination of Robert Thurston. Staff Recommendation: #1 - Approve the nomination of Robert Thurston Recommended Motion: I move to approve Robert Thurston as the recipient of the 2026 Jack Perry Award. Attachments: 1. Resolution 13-R-04 008 June 27, 2026 To the Esteemed Members of the Jack Perry Award Committee, I am writing to nominate Lakeland resident Robert Thurston for the 2026 Jack Perry Award. Mr. Thurston has a long history of service to the City of College Park and beyond. I became aware of the depth and breadth of his dedication while serving as a District 2 City Council representative, but my initial introduction was to his role as president of the Lakeland Civic Association. At the beginning of my tenure on council, the Lakeland Civic Association meetings were often small, and the leadership consisted of the president and treasurer. Still, Mr. Thurston continued the work of monitoring policies and actions that might affect Lakeland and keeping attendees informed. When news broke about the redevelopment of Campus Village Shopping Center, attendance, and feelings, increased dramatically. Mr. Thurston managed that transition with poise, humility, inclusiveness and compassion. With the partnership of Vice President Ruth Murphy, volunteers from the University of Maryland, and others, he modernized the LCA. He built a website to keep Lakelanders aware of upcoming events and meeting agendas and provided virtual access to meetings so members of the Lakeland diaspora could attend. Much like Jack Perry, his service has extended far beyond his neighborhood. He has served in multiple capacities that benefit the city and the region. In fact, Mr. Thurston has served in so many roles for so long that I fear I will neglect to mention some, but I will do my best. In addition to being Lakeland Civic Association president, he has served on the Restorative Justice Commission, Ethics Committee, Senior Advisory Committee, the Age-Friendly College Park Workgroup, Affordable Housing Task Force and the Purple Line Corridor Coalition. In addition, he chairs Neighbors Helping Neighbors of College Park. His work across these groups serves residents of all ages in every district of College Park and has contributed to more equitable policies beyond our borders. A couple years ago, I saw a truck had stopped to help a person whose car had broken down on Greenbelt Road. I was not surprised to see Mr. Thurston providing assistance. This is who he is. In addition to personally serving in these diverse and impactful roles, he has inspired his children to do the same, which positively impacts the city across generations. In closing, Mr. Thurston has given countless hours of his time to make College Park a better place for all, and he has done so quietly, without the need for recognition or praise. While he might demur from being recognized with the Jack Perry Award, I think it is crucial to acknowledge and celebrate the citizens who work hard to make our city better. College Park is a stronger city and has a brighter future due to Mr. Thurston’s service. My hope is that recognizing him inspires others. Thank you for your time and consideration and for creating this award that memorializes Jack Perry’s contribution to College Park and recognizes others who do the same. text: Public Comment Tuesday, October 27, 2026 26-G-103 Sent: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 2:07 PM To: cpmc <cpmc@collegeparkmd.gov> Subject: Age Friendly Action Plan Dear Members of City Council, | would like to endorse the Age Friendly College Park Action Plan, and in particular three of the priorities that have been identified. Unmet transportation needs: this is my highest priority. Current limitations for rides are limited to Prince Georges County and a radius of 8 miles. | strongly encourage you to use vouchers for Uber or Lyft for rides that go beyond these limits. | know other cities have done this. As we age and it become harder to drive, transportation to medical appointments can be a major part of our wellbeing. Support for home repair assistance. | urge you to consider not just monetary assistance for repairs. Especially helpful would be a vetted list of contractors and individuals who could do home repairs, from simple handyman climbing a ladder to replace batteries for smoke detectors to roofers and appliance repair people. Support for caregivers. Caring for a sick family member, especially over an extended period of time takes a huge toll on the caregiver. Providing respite for caregivers is much needed. | hope to see support for this action plan and hope that there will be meaningful allocations for these items in next year's budget. Sincerely, Harriet McNamee Worksession A. Budget From: Annie O'Connell Sent: Tuesday, October 27, 2026 3:50 PM To: comc <cpmc@collegeparkmd.gov> Subject: Public Comment for the Council Meeting Tonight Hello Mayor and Council. My name is Annie O'Connell, and | live in College Park District 2. lam writing to address the budget discussion today. The city council should not spend its budget on creating a new College Park Police Department, nor should they spend it on increased surveillance. | think this for several reasons: 1.) There is no demand for a new police department. We are already policed by 5 agencies, and crime is the lowest it's been in about 20 years according to state data. 2.) As a student and alum of the University of Maryland, | have seen police be used to intimidate students and suppress free speech on campus and adjacent to campus, including on Baltimore Avenue. Adding a College Park force will add fuel to the fire. 3.) At the council meeting on policing, UMPD reported that a police force would NOT be an appropriate way to address mental health concerns, instead pointing to UMD's deescalation team. 4. Surveillance is NOT a good alternative because in addition to individual abuses by police against civilians, ICE is known to use city, county, and state license plate readers to target immigrants. 5,) At College Park Day, as a member of the Committee for a Better Environment, | asked members of the public what there favorite part of being outside in the City was. Many people answered that their favorite thing was safe parks and outdoor urban spaces to meet up with friends and hang out. They spoke about feeling safe outside despite the fact that we don't currently have our own police force. Police cannot eliminate crime or risk, and having another entity surveilling us and enforcing laws like "no loitering”, incorrect permitting, underage drinking, etc will make College Park feel more unwelcoming and unsafe. Instead of more police, College Park should invest in real public safety in the form of improved road infrastructure, crossing guards at local schools, flood mitigation and wetland protection, and non-carceral (non-police) mental health services. At the last meeting, | mentioned | would be happy to facilitate discussions with the public as part of the policing study. | look forward to hearing back from the team, as | have not heard back yet. Thank you, Annie O'Connell Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 6, 2026 Page 1 MINUTES College Park City Council Meeting Tuesday, October 6, 2026 7:30 p.m. HYBRID In Person in Council Chambers of City Hall Virtual over Zoom: https://zoom.us/j/92398574069 PRESENT: Mayor Kabir; Mayor Pro Tem Mackie; Councilmembers Hernandez, Hew (8:48pm, Zoom), Jordan, Simmons, Oates, Ranker, and Mitchell. ABSENT: None ALSO PRESENT: Kenneth Young, City Manager; Michelle Bailey Hedgepeth, Deputy City Manager; Laura Reams, Assistant City Manager; Yvette Allen, City Clerk; Melissa Flores, Assistant City Clerk; Stephanie Anderson, City Attorney; Rehanna Barre, Economic Development Coordinator; Miriam Bader, Director of Planning; Emma Martin, Student Liaison. Mayor Kabir opened the meeting at 7:30 p.m. Announcements and Comments The Mayor, Council, City Manager, and Student Liaison shared announcements regarding upcoming events, recent activities, and community programs. PROCLAMATIONS AND AWARDS The Mayor presented the following proclamations: Breast Cancer Awareness Month Grant for Safe Schools Day Indigenous Peoples Day PUBLIC COMMENT David Dorsch, resident, urged the City to sell the vacant property at 4704 Calvert Road, stating that the City should not serve as a landlord. He also questioned the removal of residents from City committees despite their regular attendance and participation. Annie O'Connell, resident, spoke in opposition to establishing a College Park police department. She cited the number of existing law enforcement agencies serving the City, declining crime trends, concerns regarding interactions with individuals with mental health conditions or disabilities, and civil rights concerns. She requested inclusion in future community outreach regarding the Public Safety Study. Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 6, 2026 Page 2 Richard Biffl, non-resident, raised concerns regarding the City’s lease-renewal ordinance and tenant waiver process. He stated that the required waiver form exceeds the ordinance, contains conflicting provisions and creates challenges for landlords seeking to offer early lease renewals to existing tenants. He requested repeal of the ordinance or revisions to the waiver requirements and form. Shelby Byrd, resident, advocated for the St. Andrews Place pedestrian safety project. She urged the City to keep the planned November presentation as scheduled and move toward the design phase, citing significant pedestrian activity, a lack of sidewalk connectivity, and the area’s high priority for sidewalk improvements. Husain Waheed, non-resident, followed up on his previous comments regarding the Transformative Economic Efficiency Initiative. He urged the City to consider formalizing or participating in the initiative, explaining that it could benefit College Park, other municipalities, and University researchers and students. He emphasized that implementation would require little to no additional staff or researcher time and would provide opportunities to apply existing research and technologies in practical settings. He offered to assist with implementation and stated that he would follow up at the next meeting. Karen Nwaogbe, resident, shared findings from a community health assessment focused on the Lakeland neighborhood. She identified concerns affecting older adults, including mental health, food insecurity, social isolation, transportation, and access to healthcare. She asked whether the City has current or planned initiatives to support the mental health and social well-being of older adults in Lakeland or throughout College Park and to address these barriers. AMENDMENTS TO AND APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA A motion was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie and seconded by Councilmember Mitchell to remove the Closed Session from the agenda. The motion passed: 7-0-0. A motion was made by Councilmember Simmons and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie to remove 26-G-98, Approval of the Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes of October 22, November 12, and December 3, 2024; and January 21, February 4, March 18, and September 9, 2025; and September 1, September 15, and September 21, 2026, from the Consent agenda to the Action Items and add: 26-G-98, Approval of the Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes of October 22, November 12, and December 3, 2024; and January 21, February 4, March 18, and September 9, 2025. 26-G-101, Approval of the Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes of September 1, September 15, and September 21, 2026 Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 6, 2026 Page 3 The motion passed: 7-0-0. A motion was made by Councilmember Mitchell and seconded by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie to approve the agenda as amended. The motion passed: 7-0-0. CONSENT AGENDA: A motion was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie and seconded by Councilmember Mitchell to approve the Consent agenda, which consisted of these items: 26-G-96 Consideration of approval of a task order under the on-call engineering services contract with Charles P. Johnson and Associates (CPJ) in the amount of $129,410.00 for the design of the Branchville Road - 51st Avenue Sidewalk Project 26-G-97 Consideration of installing a Stop Sign on Marlbrough Court at Marlbrough Way 26-R-03 Approval of Variance Application number CPV-2026-01 from §27-11002 of the Prince George's County Zoning Ordinance to permit construction of a single- width driveway/parking pad that encroaches in front of the house for property located at 9733 Narragansett Parkway The motion passed: 7-0-0. PRESENTATIONS: Update on Early Lease Ordinance Implementation Deputy City Manager Michelle Bailey Hedgepeth provided an update on the Early Lease Ordinance and its implementation. She reported that the City continues to refine the process and addresses concerns from both landlords and tenants, including informal complaints from University of Maryland student tenants who felt pressured to make lease decisions very early in their tenancy. Deputy City Manager Hedgepeth clarified lease-renewal requirements and encouraged landlords to provide clear written deadlines, allow tenants the required time to consider offers, avoid pressuring tenants, and maintain appropriate records. Deputy City Manager Hedgepeth explained that complaints may be submitted by phone, email, or through the City’s ELO Coordinator, Ms. Rehanna Barre. Although anonymous complaints may be investigated, a formal complaint supported by an affidavit is generally necessary for enforcement action. She noted that many tenants have been reluctant to file formal complaints despite raising concerns informally. The City has completed internal training, continues outreach and communication to landlords and tenants, and is working to improve implementation. Mayor and Council Meeting Minutes October 6, 2026 Page 4 The Mayor and Council thanked Deputy City Manager Michelle Bailey Hedgepeth for the update and acknowledged the ordinance’s intended purpose and discussed limitations in its implementation.,Council discussed remaining challenges, including the absence of good-cause provisions, and expressed support for continuing to review and improve the ordinance and its implementation. PUBLIC HEARING None ACTION ITEMS: 26-G-99 Approval of the Four Cities Agenda Items City Clerk Yvette Allen discussed the upcoming Four Cities meeting scheduled for October 29 in New Carrollton and asked the Mayor and Council to identify two topics they would like to have included on the Four Cities agenda. Mayor and Council discussed selecting the City’s two agenda items for the upcoming Four Cities Coalition meeting. After discussion, Council agreed to defer the topic of ADU regulations and safeguards for possible consideration at a future meeting. Council instead selected two school- related topics: a presentation from Prince George's County Public Schools regarding school transportation, including bus and bus-stop issues, and an opportunity to hear from candidates for the District 2 Board of Education seat regarding transportation and other school-related matters. A motion was made by Mayor Pro Tem Mackie and seconded by Councilmember Hernandez to approve the following two topics for submission as the City's agenda items for the Four Cities Coalition meeting to be held in New Carrollton. 1. Invite the candidates for the District 2 Board of Education to discuss transportation and other school-related matters. 2. Request a PGCPS presentation on school transportation, including bus and bus- stop issues. text: HAGERSTOWN BOARD OF ZONING APPEALS AGENDA DATE: Wednesday, October 21, 2026, 4:00 pm LOCATION: 1st Floor Meeting Room, City Hall Please visit the City’s website at www.hagerstownplanning.org for information about this meeting. The properties involved have been posted with hearing posters and two legal advertisements appeared in the Herald-Mail. Case No. Z-2025-08 – To hear an application made by Gideon Properties for a special exception for a child day care center and a variance to reduce the minimum required lot area for a special exception use from 20,000 square feet to 10,695 square feet for an infant-only daycare center with no outdoor play area at the property located at 382 South Cleveland Avenue in the RMED Zoning District, per Sections D.5.a, U, and Z of the Zoning Ordinance. Deliberations – Other Business Adjourn - Next Meeting: November 12, 2026 – 7:00 p.m. NOTICE Pursuant to the Maryland Open Meetings Law, notice is hereby given that the deliberations of the Board of Zoning Appeals are open to the public. The Board, at its discretion, may render a decision as to some or all of the cases at the hearing described above or at a subsequent meeting or hearing, the date and time of which will be announced prior to the conclusion of the public hearing. Individuals requiring special accommodation are requested to contact the City Clerk at 301-739-8577, extension 113 or ADD 301- 797-6617. CITY OF HAGERSTOWN Department of Planning & Economic Development InvestHagerstown.org 32 N. Potomac, Suite 200 Hagerstown, Maryland 21740 Planning 301-766-4058 Economic Development 301-766-4171 HAGERSTOWN BOARD OF ZONING APPEALS STAFF REPORT CASE NUMBER: Z-2025-08 HEARING DATE: APPLICANT: Gideon Properties LLC ZONING: RMED (Residential-Medium Density) SITE LOCATION: 382 S. Cleveland Ave October 21, 2026 REQUEST: 1. Variance to reduce the minimum required lot are for a special exception use from 20,000 square feet to 10,695 square feet. 2. Special exception for the use of an infant day care center with no outdoor play area within the property. DEADLINE FOR WRITTEN DECISION: December 4, 2026 STAFF REPORT (Staff comments in bold italics): 1. Variance Criteria (Article 4, Section U.8.b. – Pages 4-144 through 4-145) b. Variances. No variance shall be approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals until and unless the Board, in its written order finds that the application complies with the following criteria: An application has been filed by the owner through legal counsel. (1) Unique Condition of Property. Where by reason of exceptional narrowness, shallowness, shape, topographical conditions, or other unusual situations or conditions peculiar to a specific parcel of property, or of the use of the property, the strict application of these regulations would result in peculiar or unusual practical difficulties to, or undue hardship upon, the owner of the property. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (1). The property has a lot size of 10,695 square feet, which is less than the minimum lot area required for a special exception use. The CITY OF HAGERSTOWN Department of Planning & Economic Development InvestHagerstown.org 32 N. Potomac, Suite 200 Hagerstown, Maryland 21740 Planning 301-766-4058 Economic Development 301-766-4171 applicant points to the mixed-use configuration of the existing building as a unique condition. (2) Minimum Necessary to Afford Relief. The variance requested is the minimum reasonably necessary to overcome the unusual conditions applicable to the property. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (2). (3) Compliance Would Preclude Common Use. That the literal interpretation of the provisions of this Ordinance would deprive the applicant of uses commonly enjoyed by other similar properties in the same district under the terms of this Ordinance. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (3). (4) No Special Privilege. That granting the variance will not confer on the applicant any special privilege that is denied by this Ordinance to other lands or structures with the same zoning. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (4). (5) Self-Created Hardship. No variance shall be granted in any case where the applicant or their agent has created or caused to be created a situation which would or has necessitated the issuance of a variance in order for such property to comply with this Ordinance. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (5). (6) Consistent with the Intent of the Ordinance. That the granting of the variance will be in harmony with the general purpose and intent of this Ordinance, and will not be injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare. The Board may prescribe appropriate and specific conditions and safeguards, including location, construction, maintenance, and operation in conformity with the Ordinance. Violation of such conditions and safeguards, when made a part of the terms under which the variance is granted, shall be a violation of this Ordinance. The applicant needs to demonstrate to the Board’s satisfaction compliance with subsection (6). Use Variances Prohibited. Under no circumstances shall the Board of Zoning Appeals grant a variance to allow a use not permissible under the terms of this ordinance in the zone involved or any use expressly or by implication prohibited by the terms of this ordinance in such zone. This provision does not apply. Day care centers are permitted by special exceptions in the RMED Zoning District. Conditions of Approval. The Board may prescribe appropriate and specific conditions and safeguards, including location, construction, maintenance, and operation in 2 conformity with this Ordinance. Violation of such conditions and safeguards, when made a part of the terms under which a variance is granted, shall be violation of this Ordinance. In this case, staff recommends two conditions 1.) The standard and required condition that the work to be performed is done consistently with the testimony provided and the application submitted, and 2.) That the applicant attempt to secure permission from the adjacent property owner to remove this property from that property and return that areas lawn condition to previous conditions if such work permission is determined. Expense of property transition from current use to original condition will be paid for by the applicant of this case. General Criteria for Special Exceptions (Article 4, Section U.7.a.(1)-(7) – Pages 140-142: (a) No special exception shall be approved by the Board of Zoning Appeals until and unless the Board finds in its written order that the application complies with the following criteria: (1) Complete Application and Documentation. A written application for a special exception is submitted by a person or persons with a financial, contractual, or proprietary interest in the property indicating the section of this ordinance under which the special exception is sought, stating the grounds on which it is requested, and including a concept plan of the proposed use which outlines the specific characteristics of the intended use on that site. A complete application and exhibit has been filed by the owner of the property. (2) Authority to Grant Special Exception and General Standards. The Board of Zoning Appeals shall make a finding that it is empowered under the section of this ordinance described in the application to grant the special exception and that the granting of the special exception will not materially or adversely affect the adjoining and surrounding properties, if: (a) the characteristics of the use and its operation on the property in question as proposed in the application or concept plan will not create any greater adverse impact than the operation of such a use on any other property with the same zoning; and (b) The proposed activity will comply with all conditions and requirements set forth for the specific use in that zoning district. In making this determination, the Board shall consider, among other things, the impact of the proposed use on neighborhood parking and traffic and whether any proposed activities will create adverse visual, dust, odor, smoke, gas, noise, or similar impact for surrounding properties. The Board is empowered to consider a special exception request for the desired use in the RMED Zoning district. However, the property does not meet the minimum area requirement for this use in this district, so for the special exception to be approved, the Board will also have to grant a variance to this requirement. The Board should consider the impact of all uses on the property in evaluating this request, since the special exception 3 use will not be the only use on the property. Also, the Board should consider the commercial nature of the building. (3) Conditions of Approval. In granting any special exception, the Board of Zoning Appeals may prescribe any special conditions in addition to those specified in the Ordinance which it feels are necessary to carry out the intent of this Ordinance and address the issues identified in (b), [2] above, so that protection of adjacent properties, the neighborhood as a whole, and the public interest are ensured. Violation of such conditions and safeguards when made a part of terms under which the special exception is granted shall be deemed a violation of this ordinance and punishable under Article 8, Section B, of this code. No comment. (4) Limited to Use Proposed to the Board. No use or activity permitted by a special exception shall be enlarged or extended beyond the limits authorized in the grant of special exception without approval of the Board. No Comment. (5) Change of Special Exception. Under no circumstances shall the Board of Zoning Appeals grant a variance to allow a use not permitted under the terms of this ordinance in the zone involved or any use expressly or by implication prohibited by the terms of this ordinance in such zone. Not applicable in this case. No special exceptions are currently in place regarding this property. (6) Use Variances or Special Exceptions for Uses Not Enumerated. Changes from one special exception use to another use permitted by special exception shall require approval by the Board. Not Applicable in this case. The proposed use is permitted by special exception and, if approved by the Board, does not constitute a “use variance.” (7) Special Criteria for this Use. None. Conditions of Approval. The Board may prescribe appropriate and specific conditions and safeguards, including location, construction, maintenance, and operation in conformity with this Ordinance. Violation of such conditions and safeguards, when made a part of the terms under which a variance is granted, shall be violation of this Ordinance. See comments regarding this issue in the section above on variances. Also, the applicant will need to demonstrate that 9’ x 18’ parking spaces are sufficient to meet ordinance requirements are being provided. 4 Other: Previous Board Action: In case Z-2020-09, the applicant applied for and obtained a similar special exception from this Board. In that case, the adjacent dwelling was under common ownership and included in the application since they proposed to use the rear yard for the day care center’s play area. A lot area variance to reduce the required minimum lot area from 20,000 square feet to 19,612 square feet was necessary and was approved by this Board. The Board approved the special exception and variance requested, but there was a condition placed on the approval that “the special exception shall be void should the properties come under separate ownership.” The applicant sold the adjoining property, voiding the prior approval. In case Z-2024-08 the applicant sought a special exception and lot area reduction variance seeking the lot area requirement be varied by nearly half. The Board denied that application via Decision and Order dated January 23, 2025. This application is substantially different than the one proposed in Z-2024-08. In this case, all children cared for are infants. There will be no outdoor play area. As such, this application does not violate the provisions of section 4.U.8., which prohibits submitting an application that is the same or similar to a denied application for one year. Parking: Special exception uses require compliance with parking requirements. This is for all uses on the property. There are 3 dwellings in the building, each requiring 2 parking spaces. A child day care center requires one space per 5 children. The applicant does not state the max number of children to be cared for. A parking space measures 9x18 feet. Assuming the number of children cared for is 20-25, the applicant will need to demonstrate they can provide 11 parking spaces on site or will have to return to this Board seeking a parking variance. Insufficient information was originally provided in the application demonstrating this has been met – the drawing being very generalized in this regard, and there is no max capacity for children cared for stated in the application. Recommendations Submitted by Boards, Commissions, and City Departments (Article 4, Section U.6): • Planning Commission: Will discuss. • Historic District Commission: Not applicable. • Board of Traffic and Parking: Not applicable. • Other Not applicable. 5
