Gregory Meekins, Dorchester County Temporary Shelter Board, expressed appreciation for the County’s contributions, support, and for the committee which was established to address these matters. Mr. Meekins emphasized the importance of assistance for individuals experiencing homelessness and noted that, in some circumstances, it is through no fault of their own. He indicated that the organization may request additional support in the future. Councilman Pfeffer explained that the CRRF refers to the distribution of cannabis tax revenues, which the State of Maryland imposes a 9% tax on sales, which 5% of the revenues collected are distributed to county governments throughout the State. Dorchester County Council Open Session Minutes of September 15, 2026 Page No. 4  Marilyn Williams, Grant Writer, highlighted a public comment, noting that recent legislation requires the committee to review relevant data to assess community needs and identify the highest-priority areas for consideration. She suggested a modification to include data related to homelessness, substance use, and mental health when evaluating community needs and assigning additional consideration to identified priority areas. Councilman Pfeffer asked for public comments. Sharon Smith, resident, inquired regarding the amount of funding available for distribution. Ms. Williams stated that the CRRF Committee will review the available funds at its September 26, 2026 meeting to determine the amount that may be released, with recommendations to be presented to the Council at its October 6, 2026 meeting. Ms. Smith asked whether the process was being conducted for the first time. Ms. Williams clarified that a similar process was conducted the previous year and noted that several years of funding had been accumulated, totaling $819,379. Upon motion by Councilman Travers, seconded by Councilman Kramer, the Council approved the CRRF Distribution Plan, with amendments, the roll call was: Pfeffer – aye; Detmer – aye; Kramer – aye; Nichols – absent; and, Travers – aye. Councilman Pfeffer asked for public comments. John Hansen, resident, asked whether the proposed plan addresses the potential for contaminants to enter the water supply. Mr. O’Donnell stated that groundwater and gas migration are monitored on a daily basis. Sharon Smith, resident, asked whether private recycling companies are subject to audits or other oversight to ensure that recyclable materials are appropriately processed and utilized. Mr. O’Donnell stated that he was uncertain regarding the extent of State-level oversight but noted that recycling practices have improved nationally. Upon motion by Councilman Travers, seconded by Councilman Detmer, the Council adopted Resolution No. 718, the roll call was: Pfeffer – aye; Detmer – aye; Kramer – aye; Nichols – absent; and, Travers – aye. text: Home / October 15, 2026 Agendas The Montgomery County Planning Board Agenda Thursday October 15, 2026 REVISED: Wednesday, October 14, 2026 - 3:07PM 9:00 am PLANNING BOARD TOUR Eastern Silver Spring Communities Plan – Planning Board Bus and Walking Tour The Planning Board will attend a tour of the Eastern Silver Spring Communities Plan area in advance of a Public Hearing scheduled in two parts on January 7 November 12 and January 14, 2027, November 19 . The purpose of the tour is educational. No Planning Board business is conducted on the tour, and no decisions can or will be made by the Planning Board during the tour. This tour is free and open to any members of the public who wish to attend as an observer and who register online; at least 15 seats are available to the public. Times provided are approximate and subject to change. The deadline to sign-up for seats on the bus was Tuesday, October 13, at 12 noon. Members of the public are welcome to meet the tour at any of the locations listed below. Please note that attendees may disembark only at Tour Locations 3 and 4. Departure – The M-NCPPC Wheaton Headquarters (2425 Reedie Drive, Wheaton, MD 20902) (9:00 am) Tour Location #1 – New Hampshire Avenue District – The Chateau Apartments / Avery Park Apartments (9:20 am) The bus will enter the roundabout on Mt. Pisgah Road and briefly stop where space allows to learn about the Draft Plan’s recommendations for the New Hampshire Avenue corridor, including improved connectivity at the New Hampshire Avenue Interchange with the Capital Beltway (I-495). Attendees will not disembark. Tour Location #2 – New Hampshire Avenue District – Northwest Park Apartments (9:45 am) The bus will travel south on New Hampshire Avenue and turn right onto Northampton Drive to learn about the Northwest Park Apartments and the Draft Plan’s recommendations for this area, including housing, parks, and trails. Attendees will not disembark. Tour Location #3 – Long Branch District and Manchester Place District (10:00 am) The bus will travel from the Northwest Park Apartments to the Long Branch Community Recreation and Senior Center. Attendees will disembark at the Center and walk across the pedestrian bridge to the Long Branch Library. From there, attendees will walk from the Long Branch Purple Line Station through Flower Avenue Urban Park and along Hartwell Road to the Manchester Place Purple Line Station. Attendees will board the bus at the intersection of Bradford Road and E. Wayne Avenue to continue the bus tour. Note: Potential restroom break at the Long Branch Community Recreation and Senior Center. Tour Location #4 – Colesville Road District (11:15 am) The bus will travel from the Manchester Place Purple Line Station to the Colesville District, including the North Hills of Sligo Creek and Indian Spring neighborhoods, to learn about the Draft Plan’s recommendations. The bus will stop at Indian Spring Terrace Local Park and attendees will briefly disembark to discuss recommendations, including the YMCA of Silver Spring. Tour Location #5 – University Boulevard District (12:00) The bus will travel from Indian Spring Terrace Local Park to the University Boulevard North District to view Eastern Middle School, the Franklin Knolls Gathering Spot, and Long Branch – Wayne Local Park (as time permits). Attendees will not disembark. This is the last stop on the tour. The bus will then return to the M-NCPPC Wheaton Headquarters. L. Stamm 12:45 pm PLANNING BOARD MEETING Item 1 Preliminary Matters *A. The subject property is located at 213 Grason Vista Dr. in the Belle Point Farm Subdivision near Queenstown MD in the 5th Election District and in the Neighborhood Conservation-1 (NC-1) Zoning District and Critical Area Limited Development Area (LDA). and WHEREAS, the Commissioners of Poolesville adopted Ordinance No. 198, effective March 3, 2014, establishing the current Zoning Ordinance of the Town of Poolesville as Appendix B of the Town Code; and WHEREAS, the Commissioners of Poolesville are authorized by §4-204 of the Land Use Article of the Code to amend, supplement, modify, or repeal sections of the Town zoning ordinance; and WHEREAS, pursuant § 4-203 of the Land Use Article of the Code, a legislative body shall hold at least one public hearing on a proposed zoning regulation or boundary at which parties in interest and citizens have an opportunity to be heard, and the legislative body shall publish notice of the time and place of the public hearing, together with a summary of the proposed zoning regulation or boundary, in at least one newspaper of general circulation in the local jurisdiction once each week for 2 successive weeks, and the legislative body shall publish the first notice of the hearing at least 14 days before the hearing, and the zoning regulation or boundary may not become effective until 10 days after the hearing or hearings.NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED, by the Commissioners of Poolesville, that the Zoning Ordinance of the Town of Poolesville, previously enacted as ORDINANCE NO. 198, as amended, is hereby amended as follows (substantive changes (additions) depicted in red text and deletions depicted in stricken text): ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 1 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ Section 1: To Amend Section 9 (Signs) (Appendix B, Part II) to add or modify the following provisions of the Sign Code: Sec. 9. Signs A. Purpose and scope. 1. The purpose of this Ordinance is to regulate all exterior signs and interior signs placed for exterior observance to protect property values, to protect the character of the Town of Poolesville, to protect health and safety, and to promote the public welfare. 2. The principal features are the restriction of advertising to the business or to the use of the premises on which the sign is located, and the restriction on the total sign area permissible per site. Any sign placed on land or on a building for the purposes of identification or for advertising a use conducted therein or thereon shall be deemed to be accessory and incidental to such land, building, or use. 3. Signs shall comply with the Architectural Guidelines and Streetscape Design as outlined in the current Poolesville Master Plan. 4. It is further intended that in commercial areas now in existence and more so in proposed commercial and industrial areas that all signs within one (1) complex be coordinated with the architecture in such a manner that the overall appearance is harmonious in color, form, and proportion. 5. Outdoor advertising signs not connected to the site or building on which they are located are prohibited. C. Signs permitted in all zones 3. Banners. A banner is a temporary means of advertising a specific event or special event, made of flexible material, and fastened at both ends. The size is limited to one and one-half (1.5) square feet for each linear foot of building frontage to which it will be attached to the building. Only one (1) banner can be displayed at any business location, not to exceed sixty (60) days within a period of three (3) months. The application for a banner showing a specific location will be submitted to the Town Manager or designee Sign Review Board for approval. *** ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 2 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ 6. Civic, religious, and quasi-public signs. Name, directional and informational signs and emblems of service clubs, places of worship, civic organizations, and quasi-public uses shall be permitted on private property if setback is in accordance with the requirements of the zoning restrictions relating to the classification of the property on which the sign is placed. Each sign shall be not more than ten (10) square feet in area. The top of such sign shall not exceed five (5) feet in height. Illumination shall be in accordance with the restrictions set forth in subsection H. hereof, and in the event that there is a need for more than one (1) sign at one(1) location, all such signs must be consolidated and confined within a single frame, subject to the review and recommendation of the Sign Review Board. D. Exceptions 2. Temporary Signs Signs for temporary use in any zone except for those signs referred to in subsection C.2.a shall comply with the following standards: (1)Location: at least 10 feet behind the street line. (2) Number (maximum): one per street the property fronts, unless modified in the sign permit. (3) Area (maximum): six square feet. 2. Temporary signs. Temporary signs, announcing any public, charitable, educational, or religious event or function, located entirely within the premises of that institution and set back no less than three (3) feet from the property line, easement, or right-of-way, whichever is the greater setback, up to a sign area of twenty-four (24) square feet. Such signs shall be allowed no more than thirty (30) days prior to the event or function and must be removed within seven (7) days after the event or function. Such signs may not be illuminated. If building mounted, these sign shall be flat wall signs and shall not project above the roofline. If ground mounted, the top shall be no more than five (5) feet above ground level. *** 6. Political campaign signs. Signs announcing candidates seeking public political office and other data pertinent thereto shall not require a permit up to a total area of nine (9) ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 3 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ square feet for each premises in a residential or commercial zone. These signs shall be confined within private property and shall not be less than fifteen (15) feet from the nearest edge of the pavement and fifty (50) feet from the nearest curb intersection of any street or road. These signs may be displayed thirty (30) days prior and seven (7) days after the election for which intended. In cases where a final election follows within seventy-five (75) days of a primary election, those candidates who won in the primary elections may continue to display their signs during the interim period and up to seven (7) days after the final election. A permit shall be required for either a freestanding or flat wall sign located at campaign headquarters only not to exceed twenty-four (24) square feet. A freestanding sign shall not exceed seven (7) feet in height and six (6) feet from the property line. A flat wall sign must be attached to the principal frontage of building. No illumination of political signs shall be permitted. *** H. Permits and fees. 1. Requirements. No sign shall be erected, altered, or relocated without a permit issued by the Town Manager or designee, Sign Review Board, except those signs listed in subsection *** K. Administration and penalties. 1. Processing. All signs of a permanent nature requiring Sign Review Board approval shall have a decision of the Board within fourteen (14) days of submission. Temporary signs or banners may be approved by the Town Manager. The Town Manager shall approve all permanent signs that meet the conditions of this section within fourteen (14) days of submission. The Town Manager may approve temporary signs or banners. *** 3. Interpretation. Where there is any ambiguity or dispute concerning the interpretation of the Ordinance, the decision of the Town Manager Sign Review Board shall prevail, subject to appeal as provided herein. *** ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 4 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ Sec. 9C. Sign Review Board. Sec 9C. Sign permit procedures A. Created; composition, appointment, and term of members. 1. There is hereby created and established a board to be called the Sign Review Board, which shall consist of three (3) members who shall be appointed by the Commissioners of Poolesville for three-year terms. Vacancies shall be filled by the Commissioners of Poolesville for the unexpired term of any member whose term becomes vacant. Members shall serve until their successors are appointed and have qualified. The chairman shall be selected by the members of the Sign Review Board. The Town Manager shall serve as liaison with the Commissioners of Poolesville and the Sign Review Board. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-512) 2. Temporary appointment. In the event that a member of the Sign Review Board should be absent and/or recuse himself, the Commissioners of Poolesville may appoint a temporary member to serve in his place. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) B. Qualifications of members. All members of the Sign Review Board shall be residents of the Town of Poolesville. C. Compensation of members. All members of the Sign Review Board shall not receive any compensation for their services. D. Powers, duties. The Sign Review Board is authorized to review and approve any application for a sign permit. The Board may grant a variance where strict application of the sign Regulations would result in peculiar and unusual practical difficulties to, or exceptional or undue hardship upon, the owners of the property or owners of said sign, provided that such variance can be granted without substantial impairment of the intent, purpose, and integrity of the regulations and of this Ordinance. This provision shall not permit the Board to grant a variance allowing any prohibited sign. (Ordinance No. 190, 65-12) E. Procedure. 1. The Town Manager or designee, Sign Review Board shall review all applications for a sign. If a determination is made that all aspects of the Sign Ordinance have been met, the pending application shall be approved. The Administrative Officer makes a determination that all aspects of the Sign Ordinance have been met, the Town Manager or designee shall approve the pending application. If the pending application requires any variance from the sign regulations, the application shall be submitted to the Sign Review Board Planning Commission for consideration and decision consistent with the provisions of the Sign Ordinance. Nothing contained herein shall ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 5 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ prevent the Town Manager from submitting any sign application to the Planning Commission for consideration and decision. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Town Manager or designee shall appeal the decision to the Planning Commission Sign Review Board within ten (10) days after the Town Manager or designee's decision is rendered. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) 2. When exercising its powers and duties, not less than two (2) members of the Sign Review Board shall constitute a quorum. The Board shall keep minutes of its proceedings and meetings. All actions or decisions of the Board shall be in written form. For assistance in reaching decisions, the Board may request technical service, advise, data, or factual evidence from the Town of Poolesville or other governmental agencies. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) F. Appeals from decisions. Any decision by the Town Manager or Planning Commission (Reviewer) Sign Review Board may, within ten (10) days after the decision is rendered, be appealed by any interested person to the Board of Zoning Appeals, which shall have the power after notice and hearing to either affirm the decision of the Sign review board Reviewer, or if it finds such decision is contrary to or inconsistent with the requirements, purposes and intent of this Ordinance, to reverse, or to remand the case to the Sign Review Board Reviewer with a written opinion setting forth the reasons for its action. Whenever any such appeal is taken, a copy thereof shall be served on the Reviewer Sign Review Board by the Town Clerk. The Reviewer Sign Review Board shall promptly give notice of the appeal to all parties to the proceedings before it and shall, within five (5) days after the filing of the appeal, file with the Board of Zoning Appeals the originals or certified copies of all paper and evidence presented to the Reviewer Sign Review Board in the proceeding before it, together with a copy of its decisions and findings. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) F. Employees. The Commissioners of Poolesville shall make available to the Sign Review Board such employees, services, or facilities of the Town as necessary. The Town of Poolesville's counsel shall serve as counsel to the Board. (Ord. No. 130, 3-6-95, Ord. No. 168, 2-21-06, Ord. No. 170, 9-17-07, Ord. No. 190; 6-5-12) *** Section 2: Severability If any section, subsection, sentence, clause, phrase, or portion of this Ordinance is for any reason held invalid or unconstitutional by any court of competent jurisdiction, such portion shall be ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 6 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ deemed a separate, distinct, and independent provision, and such holding shall not affect the validity of the remaining portions of this Ordinance. Section 3: Effect on Other Provisions. All other provisions of Appendix B, “Zoning,” of the Code of the Town of Poolesville, and all other ordinances of the Town of Poolesville, shall remain in full force and effect except as specifically amended herein. Section 4: Effective Date. This Ordinance shall take effect on ___, 20__, or on the date of its enactment by the Commissioners of Poolesville, whichever is later. APPROVED THIS __ DAY OF ___, 2026. ___ James E. Brown, President Commissioners of Poolesville A TRUE COPY ATTEST: ___ Margaret A. Leibrand, Town Clerk ___ Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 7 of 7 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. ___ MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING THIS MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING (the “MOU”) is entered into as of September 30, 2026, by and between the TOWN OF POOLESVILLE, MARYLAND (the “Town”), a municipal corporation and political subdivision of the State of Maryland, and JOSEPH GRIMSBY and DINA VULPIS (the “Grimsby-Vulpis Family”). RECITALS WHEREAS, the Grimsby-Vulpis Family wishes to honor the memory of their son, Dakota Grimsby, by establishing a crowdfunding campaign via GoFundMe (the “Campaign”) to raise funds from the community to enhance pedestrian and traffic safety in the Town of Poolesville; and WHEREAS, the Town Commissioners have expressed their formal support for this initiative and their commitment to partnering with the Grimsby-Vulpis Family to protect residents and visitors; and WHEREAS, both parties desire to establish a clear, transparent framework for the direct receipt, restricted accounting, and lawful expenditure of these community-donated funds. NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants contained herein, the parties agree as follows: 1. ESTABLISHMENT OF THE CAMPAIGN AND DIRECT BENEFICIARY STATUS   Platform Setup: The Grimsby-Vulpis Family shall establish the GoFundMe campaign under the title “The Dakota Grimsby Memorial Traffic Safety Fund.” Direct Payouts: To ensure transparency and compliance with crowdfunding guidelines, the Grimsby-Vulpis Family shall designate the Town of Poolesville as the direct, exclusive financial beneficiary within the GoFundMe platform. No campaign funds shall pass through any personal bank account of the Grimsby-Vulpis Family. 2. CREATION OF A DEDICATED MUNICIPAL FUND   Restricted Accounting: Upon receipt of the electronic payouts from GoFundMe, the Town shall deposit all campaign proceeds into a distinct, restricted, or dedicated accounting fund separated from the Town's General Fund. Fund Designation: This account shall be designated as the “Dakota Grimsby Memorial Traffic Safety Fund” (the “Fund”). 3. PERMITTED USES OF THE FUND  Primary Scope: The Town agrees that monies deposited into the Fund shall be utilized exclusively for traffic safety initiatives, pedestrian protection infrastructure, and enhanced law enforcement or public safety presence within the Town of Poolesville.   Poolesville Day Focus: In alignment with the intent of the donors, the Town shall make every reasonable administrative and contractual effort to coordinate with the appropriate law enforcement agencies to deploy a visible police presence during the hours following Poolesville Day events, funded by the Fund. Alternative Allocation: If administrative, contractual, or legal constraints prevent the execution of specialized police presence following Poolesville Day, the Town Manager, in consultation with the Grimsby-Vulpis Family, may allocate the funds toward other permanent pedestrian traffic safety improvements within the Town. 4. ADMINISTRATIVE AND REPORTING TRANSPARENCY   Tax Documentation: The Town acknowledges that it is a political subdivision capable of receiving tax-deductible contributions under Internal Revenue Code Section 170(c)(1). The Town shall provide necessary administrative confirmation or receipts to donors upon lawful request, subject to platform data availability. No Administrative Fees: The Town agrees to apply 100% of the net funds received from the platform (after standard GoFundMe processing fees) directly to the safety initiatives outlined in Section 3, without deducting municipal administrative overhead costs. 5. TERM AND TERMINATION  This MOU shall become effective upon signature by all parties and shall remain in effect until the Fund has been fully expended for its intended purposes, or unless terminated or amended sooner by mutual written agreement of both parties. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties hereto have executed

ORDINANCE NO. 237 INTRODUCED: SEPT 21, 2026 PUBLIC HEARING: October 5, 2026 EFFECTIVE : An Ordinance to Amend Section 9 (Signs) (Appendix B, Part II) of the Town’s Zoning Ordinance WHEREAS, pursuant to Section 82.12(65) of the Charter of the Town of Poolesville, Maryland, Title 4 of the Land Use Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland, and applicable provisions of the Code of the Town of Poolesville, the Commissioners of the Town of Poolesville are empowered to exercise planning and zoning powers within the Town of Poolesville, Maryland; and WHEREAS, the Commissioners of Poolesville adopted Ordinance No. 198, effective March 3, 2014, establishing the current Zoning Ordinance of the Town of Poolesville as Appendix B of the Town Code; and WHEREAS, the Commissioners of Poolesville are authorized by §4-204 of the Land Use Article of the Code to amend, supplement, modify, or repeal sections of the Town zoning ordinance; and WHEREAS, pursuant § 4-203 of the Land Use Article of the Code, a legislative body shall hold at least one public hearing on a proposed zoning regulation or boundary at which parties in interest and citizens have an opportunity to be heard, and the legislative body shall publish notice of the time and place of the public hearing, together with a summary of the proposed zoning regulation or boundary, in at least one newspaper of general circulation in the local jurisdiction once each week for 2 successive weeks, and the legislative body shall publish the first notice of the hearing at least 14 days before the hearing, and the zoning regulation or boundary may not become effective until 10 days after the hearing or hearings.NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED, by the Commissioners of Poolesville, that the Zoning Ordinance of the Town of Poolesville, previously enacted as ORDINANCE NO. 198, as amended, is hereby amended as follows (substantive changes (additions) depicted in red text and deletions depicted in stricken text): Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Purpose and scope. 1. The purpose of this Ordinance is to regulate all exterior signs and interior signs placed for exterior observance to protect property values, to protect the character of the Town of Poolesville, to protect health and safety, and to promote the public welfare. 2. The principal features are the restriction of advertising to the business or to the use of the premises on which the sign is located, and the restriction on the total sign area permissible per site. Any sign placed on land or on a building for the purposes of identification or for advertising a use conducted therein or thereon shall be deemed to be accessory and incidental to such land, building, or use. 3. Signs shall comply with the Architectural Guidelines and Streetscape Design as outlined in the current Poolesville Master Plan. 4. It is further intended that in commercial areas now in existence and more so in proposed commercial and industrial areas that all signs within one (1) complex be coordinated with the architecture in such a manner that the overall appearance is harmonious in color, form, and proportion. 5. Outdoor advertising signs not connected to the site or building on which they are located are prohibited. C. Signs permitted in all zones 2. Temporary real estate signs a. Temporary real estate yard signs on posts shall not exceed six (6) square feet in area and seven (7) feet in height, located on the subject property and limited to one (1) such sign for each frontage of a home, lot, parcel, or tract. Signs shall be removed within ten (10) days of the sale. Directional signs announcing active and current home and property sale activity may be placed in the public right-of-way on weekends between the hours of 4:00 PM Friday and 7:00 AM on the following Monday and shall not exceed three (3) square feet in area and five (5) in number per home or property. Directional signs are limited to being placed on street corners to direct traffic specifically to an active and current home or property sale. Directional signs are limited to one per intersection. However, if in the opinion of a police officer, signs so placed constitute a hazard to traffic, the police officer may remove such sign. These signs are expressly exempt from a permit requirement. Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 2 of 8 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. 3. Banners. A banner is a temporary means of advertising a specific event or special event, made of flexible material, and fastened at both ends. The size is limited to one and one-half (1.5) square feet for each linear foot of building frontage to which it will be attached to the building. Only one (1) banner can be displayed at any business location, not to exceed sixty (60) days within a period of three (3) months. The application for a banner showing a specific location will be submitted to the Town Manager or designee Sign Review Board for approval. *** Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. Page 3 of 8 Town of Poolesville Ordinance No. 6. Civic, religious, and quasi-public signs. Name, directional and informational signs and emblems of service clubs, places of worship, civic organizations, and quasi-public uses shall be permitted on private property if setback is in accordance with the requirements of the zoning restrictions relating to the classification of the property on which the sign is placed. Each sign shall be not more than ten (10) square feet in area. The top of such sign shall not exceed five (5) feet in height. Illumination shall be in accordance with the restrictions set forth in subsection H. hereof, and in the event that there is a need for more than one (1) sign at one(1) location, all such signs must be consolidated and confined within a single frame, subject to the review and recommendation of the Sign Review Board. D. Exceptions 2. Temporary Signs Signs for temporary use in any zone except for those signs referred to in subsection C.2.a shall comply with the following standards: (1) Location: at least 10 feet behind the street line. (2) Number (maximum): one per street the property fronts, unless modified in the sign permit. (3) Area (maximum): six square feet. 2. Temporary signs. Temporary signs, announcing any public, charitable, educational, or religious event or function, located entirely within the premises of that institution and set back no less than three (3) feet from the property line, easement, or right-of-way, whichever is the greater setback, up to a sign area of twenty-four (24) square feet. Such signs shall be allowed no more than thirty (30) days prior to the event or function and must be removed within seven (7) days after the event or function. Such signs may not be illuminated. If building mounted, these sign shall be flat wall signs and shall not project above the roofline. If ground mounted, the top shall be no more than five (5) feet above ground level. *** 6. Political campaign signs. Signs announcing candidates seeking public political office and other data pertinent thereto shall not require a permit up to a total area of nine (9) Asterisks * * * : Indicate that text is retained from existing law but omitted herein. These signs shall be confined within private property and shall not be less than fifteen (15) feet from the nearest edge of the pavement and fifty (50) feet from the nearest curb intersection of any street or road. These signs may be displayed thirty (30) days prior and seven (7) days after the election for which intended. In cases where a final election follows within seventy-five (75) days of a primary election, those candidates who won in the primary elections may continue to display their signs during the interim period and up to seven (7) days after the final election. A permit shall be required for either a freestanding or flat wall sign located at campaign headquarters only not to exceed twenty-four (24) square feet. There is hereby created and established a board to be called the Sign Review Board, which shall consist of three (3) members who shall be appointed by the Commissioners of Poolesville for three-year terms. Vacancies shall be filled by the Commissioners of Poolesville for the unexpired term of any member whose term becomes vacant. Members shall serve until their successors are appointed and have qualified. The chairman shall be selected by the members of the Sign Review Board. The Town Manager shall serve as liaison with the Commissioners of Poolesville and the Sign Review Board. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-512) 2. Temporary appointment. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) B. Qualifications of members. All members of the Sign Review Board shall be residents of the Town of Poolesville. C. Compensation of members. The Sign Review Board is authorized to review and approve any application for a sign permit. The Board may grant a variance where strict application of the sign Regulations would result in peculiar and unusual practical difficulties to, or exceptional or undue hardship upon, the owners of the property or owners of said sign, provided that such variance can be granted without substantial impairment of the intent, purpose, and integrity of the regulations and of this Ordinance. This provision shall not permit the Board to grant a variance allowing any prohibited sign. (Ordinance No. 190, 65-12) E. Procedure. 1. (Ordinance No. 190; 6-5-12) 2. When exercising its powers and duties, not less than two (2) members of the Sign Review Board shall constitute a quorum. The Board shall keep minutes of its proceedings and meetings. All actions or decisions of the Board shall be in written form. Whenever any such appeal is taken, a copy thereof shall be served on the Reviewer Sign Review Board by the Town Clerk. The Reviewer Sign Review Board shall promptly give notice of the appeal to all parties to the proceedings before it and shall, within five (5) days after the filing of the appeal, file with the Board of Zoning Appeals the originals or certified copies of all paper and evidence presented to the Reviewer Sign Review Board in the proceeding before it, together with a copy of its decisions and findings. title: October 05, 2026, Agenda for the October 5, 2026, Commissioners Meeting. Minutes
text: APPROVED OCTOBER 19, 2026 MINUTES COMMISSIONERS OF POOLESVILLE October 5, 2026 *** This meeting was conducted live and streamed with live time posting to YouTube. Notice of the meeting date, time, and agenda were posted in advance, physically at the Town Hall, on the Town’s Website, and on social media. Before the start of the meeting, it was confirmed that the public could view the meeting on YouTube. Call to Order: President Brown called the meeting to order at 6:00 PM Commissioners Reed, Paksima, Bupp and Hobbs were in attendance. Town Manager Yost (virtual) was also in attendance. Adjourn to Closed Session: Commissioner Reed motioned to adjourn to a closed session pursuant to State Article 3-305(b)(i) to interview Town Manager candidates. Second by Commissioner Paksima. Motion carries 5-0. Call to Order: President Brown called the meeting to order at 7:00 PM Commissioners Reed (virtual), Paksima, Bupp and Hobbs were in attendance. Town Manager Yost (virtual) and Assistant Manager Anderegg were also in attendance. Pledge of Allegiance: Commissioner Paksima led the Pledge of Allegiance. Public Hearing: President Brown read the opening statement for Ordinance NO 237 – Sign Code Amendments. Jerry Klobukowski discussed the changes and recommended adding a manager designee to the approval process. President Brown offered some clarifying amendments to the real estate sign section. Commissioner Reports/Announcements: Commissioner Hobbs discussed the Halmos Park parking pad and pedestrian safety bills. Commissioner Bupp discussed the October agenda including Town Code definitions and a property subdivision. Commissioner Paksima reported that Fair Access will be meeting on October 15 and discussed 2 MCPS presentations, school closure process, world branding program, economic development in the Ag reserve and the Poolesville Day breakfast video. Commissioner Reed discussed the agenda for the October meeting, recycling event and Rise against Hunger. President Brown discussed the recycling event and shred truck and Whites Ferry. Public Comment None Approval of Minutes Commissioner Paksima motioned to approve the September 21, 2026, minutes. Second, by Commissioner Bupp. Motion carried 5-0. New Business Dakota Grimsby GoFundMe MOU – Assistant Manager Anderegg provided the introduction. After a short discussion, Commissioner Paksima motioned to approve the MOU. Second by Commissioner Hobbs. Motion carried 5-0. Seneca Pump Station Generator – Assistant Manager Anderegg briefed the Commissioners on the condition and need for new generator at the sewage pump station. After a brief discussion, Commissioner Bupp motioned to transfer $60,000 from the Unrestricted Reserves account to Account #3150 for the purchase and installation of a generator at the Seneca Pump Station. Second by Commissioner Reed. Motion carried 5-0. Old Business: Ordinance NO. 236 – Use of Golf Carts on Municipal Roadways: Assistant Manager Anderegg provided a summary of the ordinance and process. Commissioner Hobbs to adopt Ordinance NO. 236. Second by Commissioner Paksima. Motion carried 5-0. Ordinance NO. 235 – Accessory Dwelling Units: Assistant Manager Anderegg provided a summary of the ordinance and process. After a discussion regarding water allocation, Commissioner Bupp motioned to adopt Ordinance NO. 235. Second by Commissioner Paksima. Motion carried 5-0. Town Manager Report Manager Yost and Assistant Manager Anderegg reported on: 1. 2. 3. Staff is winding down the design phase for the streetscape and preparing for the construction/bid Phase. The basin recoating at the WWTP was coming to a close. A production company will be using Dr. Dillingham Park for staging. Adjournment Commissioner Bupp motioned to adjourn. Second by Commissioner Reed. Motion carried 5-0. REPORT-IN-BRIEF: Proclamation Presentation WHEREAS, Domestic Violence Awareness Month is intended to draw attention to the fact that domestic violence is widespread and has public health implications for every community member of Washington County, and; WHEREAS, we must work together to educate our community on how to prevent domestic violence and how to support survivors. Staff and volunteers of anti-violence programs in Washington County encourage every person to speak out when witnessing acts of violence. Through prevention education and increased awareness, there is compelling evidence that we can be successful in reducing domestic violence in Washington County and hold perpetrators who commit acts of violence responsible for their actions, and; WHEREAS, Washington County strongly supports the efforts of the national, state and local partners and of every citizen to actively engage in public and private efforts, including conversations about what domestic violence is, how to prevent it, and how to help survivors connect with services. NOW THEREFORE, we the Board of County Commissioners of Washington County, Maryland, hereby recognize the month of October as “Domestic Violence Awareness Month” and encourage all citizens to speak out against domestic violence and support efforts to educate young people about healthy relationships centered on respect, support victims and survivors, and to support the efforts of victim advocates, service providers, health care providers, and the legal system in working to end domestic violence. Taylor Director MINUTES The Wicomico County Planning and Zoning Commission (“Commission”) met in regular session on September 17, 2026, in Room 301, Council Chambers, Government Office Building, with the following persons participating: COMMISSION MEMBERS: Charles “Chip” Dashiell, Chairman Sara Bynum-King Mandel Copeland Jim Thomas PLANNING STAFF: Tracey Taylor, Wicomico County Department of Planning, Zoning, and Community Development (“PZCD”) Janae Merchant, Recording Secretary, PZCD Clark Meadows, PZCD Colin Harrison, PZCD Becky Thayne, PZCD Gabby Carr, Wicomico County Department of Law Chairman Dashiell called the meeting to order at 4:00 p.m. and noted the absences of Ms. Tanesha Siggers and Mr. Daniel Moreno-Holt. MINUTES: The County minutes from the August 20, 2026, meeting were brought forward for approval. Chairman Dashiell noted that since Ms. Sara Bynum-King and Mr. Jim Thomas were not present at the previous meeting, the minutes would be approved and/or revised via email to Ms. Janae Merchant. Chairman Dashiell requested that all individuals who planned to provide testimony before the Commission stand and be sworn in; Ms. Gabby Carr administered the Oath. Minutes – September 17, 2026 Page |2 COMMISSIONERS VOTE – AMENDED ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT – An Act to amend Chapter 225 of the Wicomico County Code, titled “Zoning,” to establish and revise regulations pertaining to the installation, construction, location, and size of solar energy systems as necessary to comply with the requirements of Acts of Maryland 2025, Chapter 623 (Maryland Senate Bill 931), Annotated Code of Maryland. (T. Taylor) Chairman Dashiell noted that although the Amended Zoning Text Amendment was introduced last month for public hearing, the Commissioners would vote on the text amendment at this meeting. Chairman Dashiell then welcomed Ms. Taylor to begin the discussion of the prepared memorandum on the solar bill. Ms. Taylor noted that although she was absent from the August meeting, Ms. Kaylee Justice, PZCD Deputy Director, and staff later provided her with updates on the public's suggested revisions to the solar bill. Ms. Taylor also noted that because an election is approaching within the next fifty days, which will result in a majority new County Council and the potential for a new County Executive, it will be challenging to pass any legislative bills in the time remaining for this current County Council. Ms. Taylor explained she reviewed the suggested changes and discussed them internally with Planning staff, and consulted with other area Planning Directors. While she respects the concerns and comments raised during the public hearing, she does not recommend incorporating the proposed revisions into the legislation as currently drafted. She stated that, in her professional judgment, several proposed revisions would create an administrative review process inconsistent with the Department’s established procedures, unnecessarily expanding staff obligations, and duplicate resources already available through the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC). Ms. Taylor further explained that solar applications must be reviewed under State regulations, which preempt local zoning authority. The Department still retains the ability to determine when legal, policy, or administrative issues warrant additional review and/or formal intervention based on the circumstances of the individual project. Ms. Taylor also expressed concern about the proposed revision requiring Planning staff to attend all meetings and hearings associated with solar projects. Ms. Taylor noted that while staff attendance at applicable public hearings is appropriate and necessary to support the regulatory review process and respond to questions within the Department’s jurisdiction, requiring attendance at every meeting is neither practical nor an efficient use of staff resources. Many public hearings are held locally, while other meetings may take place across the Bay Bridge. Given the geographic locations, travel requirements, and existing responsibilities of Department staff, it is not reasonable to expect staff to attend every meeting associated with a solar project. As a practical alternative to the final suggested revision to keep a local database of all County solar projects, Ms. Taylor offered dedicated solar energy information on the Department’s website, including a link to the PSC portal to help residents access solar project documentation. Additionally, the Department’s existing GIS tracking of solar projects can also be made readily accessible through the County’s online Map Room. This approach would improve public access to information while avoiding duplicative document management already supported through the Public Service Commission website. Ms. Taylor then informed the Commissioners of notations to the legislative bill, stating that the County Law Department added blue comments and that Ms. Taylor recommended the red comments. Additional items were struck, eliminated, and/or reworded to adjust the language to fit appropriately for the County’s adoption of this solar text amendment. Ms. Taylor then invited Mr. Clark Meadows, the Zoning Administrator, to address the Commissioners with potential zoning questions regarding solar projects. Mr. Meadows stated that the County previously had final approval for solar projects and did not require the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) before adopting Senate Bill 931. The Board Minutes – September 17, 2026 Page |3 of Appeals previously reviewed this process by special exception and applied it to solar projects up to 2 megawatts. Now, since Senate Bill 931 passed, the State supersedes solar application approval in the County, regardless of the utility scale of solar projects. Considering State and local legislation, Ms. Taylor also acknowledged the development of solar projects in relation to the Priority Preservation Area (PPA). State law allows solar projects up to 5% of the County's PPA. The PPA is the entire A1 zoning district. Ms. Taylor also noted that representatives at the most recent Maryland Association of Counties (MACo) meeting said they would not consider a statewide solar revision bill this legislative session to decrease that percentage from 5% to the recommended 2%. Nonetheless, staff will thoroughly review all solar project applications that comply with State regulations and local County ordinances, as permitted by State law. Finally, Ms. Taylor acknowledged staff collaboration and input before presenting the amended bill to the Planning Commission and County Council. Regarding the public hearing at the last meeting, Ms. Bynum-King and Mr. Jim Thomas commended Ms. Taylor and staff for their due diligence in addressing concerns about the Zoning Text Amendment. Although there was no public hearing at this meeting, Chairman Dashiell welcomed Mr. Nathaniel Morton, who lives on Union Church Road and attended the previous meeting, to make additional comments. Ms. Morton thanked the County Attorney and staff for considering public comments before voting on the Zoning Text Amendment. Mr. Morton reiterated the importance of the County intervening in ongoing meetings and hearings to review local solar projects. To support his point, Mr. Morton distributed handouts of an aerial map of CPCN solar handout sites within 3 miles of Nanticoke Road, which specifically highlighted solar project Case #9806. Although County staff attended the second public hearing for this solar project, the PSC held an evidentiary hearing at its headquarters in Baltimore the same day. Wicomico County did not petition to intervene and therefore did not have an opportunity to voice its decision for Case #9806 at Nanticoke Road. Mr. Morton also stated that the judge of the Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), a division of the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR), recently questioned the review of Case #9806. Mr. Morton's map showed solar projects submitted to the Power Plant Research Program (PPRP) for the pre-application process. This allows affected counties and municipalities to be notified at least 90 days before the CPCN is filed. Mr. Morton then provided examples of pre-application solar projects, including a 51-acre site located east of Allen Volunteer Fire Department. Mr. Morton then asked the Commissioners to consider Rulemaking 97 for the current PSC, which is solely limited to solar facilities. Rulemaking 97 would allow the County to play a larger role in the application review process, shorten the pre-application period to 30 days, and proceed without an evidentiary hearing. Mr. Morton thinks it would benefit developers, state agencies, and local government to notify neighboring landowners of the County’s decisions on solar projects. Mr. Morton again suggested that staff should petition to intervene and attend public hearings, regardless of whether staff approves of or opposes the proposed solar projects. Chairman Dashiell thanked Mr. Morton for his comments and welcomed others to be heard, despite the public hearing not taking place. As there were no additional comments, Chairman Dashiell requested a motion to forward a favorable recommendation to the Wicomico County Council on the proposed solar legislation incorporating the revisions proposed by the Wicomico County Planning Director, Tracey Taylor, and as attached to her Memorandum. Upon an motion by Ms. Bynum-King to approve the Amended Zoning Text Amendment, seconded by Mr. Thomas, the motion was duly carried. Chairman Dashiell stated the motion was APPROVED. MINOR SUBDIVISION PLAT – Lands of Gayle Basch – Gayle A. Basch, rep by Wilkins-Noble – Wango Road – A-1 Agricultural-Rural – M0050, G0022, P0054 (B. Thayne) Minutes – September 17, 2026 Page |4 Ms. Thayne and Mr. Ronald Bash, owner of 33414 Wango Road, approached the table. Ms. Thayne presented the Staff Report. The minor subdivision plat for the lands of Gayle Basch proposes creating a fourth lot from a parent parcel, subject to full Planning Commission review. In this case, the plat also creates lot three. Once lot three is established, lot four will consist of a 2-acre parcel. A previous iteration of this plat was approved by the Planning Commission in 2024. Since then, a Text Amendment to the subdivision regulations changed the 50% open space requirement lot threshold from three lots to seven lots. Until recently, Mr. Basch stated he had not planned on developing the property. However, because of the change in the open space requirements, he decided to subdivide the property and wait three years for approval of the open space text amendment so there would no longer be a 50% open space requirement. Both lots three and four meet the minimum standards per the subdivision code and the zoning code. The subdivision plat has Health Department approval and a Forest Conservation Exemption. Though the Department of Public Works has reviewed the plat, Planning staff recommends approval of the final draft of the plat as presented with the following two (2) conditions: 1. The Final Subdivision Plat shall comply with all Record Plat requirements of the Wicomico County Subdivision Regulations. 2. This approval is subject to further review and pproval and conditions imposed by the Planning and Zoning and Public Works Departments. As there were no additional comments, Chairman Dashiell requested a motion to approve the Minor Subdivision plat for the Lands of Gayle Basch, subject to the two (2) conditions outlined in the Staff Report. Upon a motion by Mr. Thomas, and seconded by Mr. Copeland, the motion was duly carried. Chairman Dashiell stated the motion was APPROVED. WORK SESSION - WICOMICO COUNTY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN UPDATE – Review of Chapter 4 (Housing Chapter) (Wallace Montgomery Staff) The Work Session began at 4:43 p.m. Chairman Dashiell noted that the Comprehensive Plan Update discussion was a Work Session; therefore, the Commissioners did not accept public comments during this portion of the meeting. The County will provide public comment opportunities through its website at a future date. Ms. Taylor then addressed the Commissioners' expectations during these Work Sessions. Because the general public will be viewing the Comprehensive Plan, Ms. Taylor reiterated the importance of noting errors and changes in the chapters as they review them. As staff reviews the chapters as they are received, Planning and Zoning staff expects feedback from the Commissioners as they are presented. They will then relay the feedback to Wallace Montgomery staff, who will prepare a final draft chapter. Additionally, a Comprehensive Plan logo is under development and will be presented to the Commissioners once finalized. Ms. Taylor also reminded the Commissioners that the Housing Chapter will include additional notes to reflect recently passed State legislation. Ms. Taylor and staff will also collaborate with the consultant to draft language reflecting these newly passed State regulations. Staff Minutes – September 17, 2026 Page |5 also decided to wait on the Land Use Chapter until after the election, but will include some Land Use references in the Housing Chapter. Chairman Dashiell expressed appreciation for staff and the planners' insights in providing brief context for the chapters being presented. Ms. Taylor then explained the importance of creating a visually appealing, informative Comprehensive Plan. The goal is to use the format that Wallace Montgomery provided moving forward, with goals, objectives, and action items for the County. Chairman Dashiell then welcomed the Commissioners' comments. Mr. Thomas commended the well-written Comprehensive Plan but noted his concerns about the gap between the plan's creators and how developers can use it to develop housing projects. He felt developers need a clearer roadmap. Ms. Taylor noted that the Housing and Land Use Chapters will differ significantly from the other chapters because newly passed State laws were not previously considered. Since the Land Use Chapter was not presented first, it would have established the foundation for how the remaining chapters are viewed. The Housing Chapter was presented before the Land Use Chapter because it addresses housing as a priority and must also consider both land use and zoning. Mr. Thomas also inquired about the definition of naturally occurring affordable housing units. Ms. Taylor explained that they are older starter homes, similar to our bungalows or ranch-style homes, and that once a family’s income allows them to move up to a more expensive home, the home they vacate becomes a naturally occurring affordable housing unit, which, in turn, is the new version of affordable housing. Ms. Bynum-King asked about the number of single-family homes converted to multi-family, and Ms. Taylor responded that she would research and report that information before or during the next meeting. Mr. Foglietta encouraged the comments from the Commissioners, whether written or submitted electronically. With no additional comments from the Commissioners at the time, Mr. Foglietta highlighted key findings in the Comprehensive Plan, including limited housing production and moderate but uneven population growth over 25 years. Some of the County's main concerns include aging infrastructure, affordable housing, and job opportunities. However, survey feedback also noted a desire for community centers and activities. Although the survey received around thirty responses, Mr. Foglietta hoped to receive more responses from younger demographics, especially the 18–24 age group. Mr. Foglietta briefly summarized concerns in the Housing Chapter based on the survey responses received so far. The Housing Chapter also highlighted five action items to prioritize housing type and density in the County. Mr. Foglietta explained the process for reviewing chapters at each meeting. Once a chapter is complete, the Commissioners will incorporate their feedback into a draft and publish it on the website for public access. Mr. Foglietta also addressed the chapter timeline, with the Transportation Chapter to be presented during the October meeting. With two Commissioners absent, Ms. Taylor suggested that Ms. Merchant send Ms. Siggers and Mr. Moreno-Holt the Housing Chapter for review to stay on schedule for the Work Sessions. Ms. Taylor stated that a recent press release included a website with a QR code that links directly to the survey webpage. The survey was also sent to various County stakeholders, including universities, non-profits, and local government. Staff will continue to promote the survey more widely. Minutes – September 17, 2026 Page |6 Additionally, Ms. Taylor noted that more affordable housing options exist in the more rural areas of our County, and that housing prices increase closer to urban centers. This creates more challenges with longer commutes and reliable transportation as the public lives farther from urban centers. Mr. Foglietta added that younger people want to access urban areas on foot and prefer to rely on public transportation. Chairman Dashiell, along with Mr. Thomas, noted that although affordable housing, reliable transportation, and longer commute times remain challenges, there are more opportunities to act and address these issues, as highlighted in the Housing Chapter. Mr. Foglietta’s final remarks emphasized the importance of the Housing and Land Use Chapters to overall public opinion. Ms. Taylor also encouraged the Commissioners to continue commenting after the chapters are published for ongoing review. The Work Session ended at 5:19 p.m. PLANNING DIRECTOR UPDATES – ( T. Taylor) Ms. Taylor provided a brief update on the following: • Kathy Smith, who attended the previous Planning Commission meeting, expressed interest in serving as a Planning Commission member. A literal interpretation of the provisions of the County’s Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area Program and related laws will deprive the applicant of rights commonly enjoyed by other properties in similar areas within the Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area; The Applicant’s rights would be lessened without the granting of this variance due to the restrictions of the Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area Program.
